item.title: Securing a Smart Dog Collar: Secure Elements, Key Lifecycles, and Why TLS Isn't Enough on 5 Microamp
item.author: Vitaliy Gribko
item.content:encoded: The key that was never really yoursYears ago I shipped a battery-powered NB-IoT pet collar and wrote about the firmware side of it: FreeRTOS, an STM32L4, safe OTA, and the small humiliations of making a radio live inside a dog's daily schedule. That article was about keeping the device alive. This one is about a question I started asking myself after the collar was already in the field, and it kept me up more than any battery budget ever did.The collar authenticated to the backend the way most small devices do: a symmetric key, provisioned at manufacture, stored on the device, stored on the server. And one evening, while re-reading my own provisioning code, I noticed the shape of what I had built. The key sat in flash. Flash can be dumped. Debug interfaces are pins on the board unless you burn the fuses, and burning them makes field diagnostics impossible. The "secret" was a file on a chip that any motivated person could read with fifty euros of hardware and a weekend.A key compiled - or flashed - into a device is not a key. It is a copy of a key, lying in the open, plus the hope that nobody looks. I had built a lock and hung the combination beside the door.This article is the class of problems behind that evening, not the story of one collar: what actually breaks when you do cryptography in software on a microcontroller, what a secure element really is (it is smaller and more boring than the marketing suggests), why key lifecycle is the actual product, and how constrained protocols do authentication on a budget of microamps. Everything here stands on public specifications and public incidents. Your threat model may differ; the physics will not.The threat model nobody puts in the quoteWhen people plan security for a small connected device, they plan for the network. TLS, certificates, maybe a VPN for the backend. When the device gets physically attacked, the standard answer is "nobody will bother with a $30 gadget."That answer aged badly in October 2016. Mir, a botnet built mostly from IP cameras and DVRs - devices nobody bothered about - took a chunk of the internet's DNS offline for an afternoon [1]. Nobody attacked those cameras because the cameras were valuable. They attacked them because the keys were default and the shells were open. Your device does not need to be a target; it needs only to be available, and to be somebody's stepping stone.For a battery-powered device, the honest threat list looks like this: The flash is readable. Keys inside firmware are keys with a deadline. One genuine device, dumped, becomes a hundred fake ones. The backend cannot tell them apart if the credential is the only identity. Capture a valid message today, send it again tomorrow. If nobody counts messages, the attack costs nothing. SWD and JTAG are wonderful for development and equally wonderful for attackers. Fusing them shut bricks your own field diagnostics. Timing and power traces leak secrets from naive software implementations. This is not theory; Kocher's paper is from 1999, which makes it older than several of my colleagues.None of this requires nation-states. It requires curiosity and a soldering iron.The anthology of shame, all public record: Mirai built its army on default credentials shipped by the million [1]. Juniper's ScreenOS carried a hardcoded admin backdoor for years (CVE-2015-7755). Fortinet's FortiOS had its "magic password" (CVE-2016-1909). An RCE in a popular camera SDK, Devil's Ivy, swept whole product families at once (CVE-2017-9765) - one shared component, one key, one compromise per product line. Sony's PS3 signing key fell not to a backdoor but to a reused nonce: the "hardware-locked" key lived in software, and software repeated itself. LoRaWAN fleets have repeatedly been found joining with default application keys straight from the manual. There is a pattern and it is not subtle: a secret that is everywhere is a secret that is nowhere.Why software crypto dies on a microcontrollerTo be clear about terms: software crypto means the secret key lives in ordinary memory - flash or RAM - and the CPU runs AES or SHA on demand. It works beautifully right up until the moment someone holds the board. A microcontroller has normal flash. Normal flash answers reads. If your code can fetch the key at boot, so can a programmer clipped to the bus. Even with the key hidden, the algorithm runs on a CPU whose power draw is visible. DPA correlates those tiny current wiggles with key bits. Kocher demonstrated it against real DES hardware when "IoT" was not yet a word. Manufacturing wants test access, support wants debug access, and shipping dates want both left enabled. Each enabled interface is a front door with a welcome mat. Bake one symmetric key into every unit of a product line, and a single compromise becomes a thousand compromised units. There is no rotation because there is no channel to rotate over that does not already assume the key.Every one of these has a public standard or a public paper behind it; none of this is secret knowledge. It is just knowledge that arrives after the board is spun, which is the worst possible order.The secure element: a smart card wearing different clothesThe host path shown here ran on a real reader and a real card while writing this piece - ATR in, SELECT out, honest status words back.The fix is older than the problem. A secure element is a smart card chip in a different package - the same technology that has lived inside bank cards and SIM cards for decades, evaluated against attack catalogs that include lasers, acid, and a microscope, and asked exactly one question: can it be made to output the key? The answer it is built to give is no.What you get, concretely:Key storage that refuses reads. The key is generated inside the chip or injected once during personalization, and there is no command that returns it. The host never sees its own key. Neither does your firmware dump.Crypto that never leaves. The applet signs, verifies, derives - you send a challenge, you get a response. The secret participates without appearing. Entropy seeded and conditioned on-chip, because the analog noise of a secure element is a better source than the ADC of a microcontroller that also has to count a dog's steps.A public, boring interface. APDU exchanges over ISO/IEC 7816-4: select an application, send a command, read two status bytes. The same protocol your bank card speaks at a terminal. On the host side, pcsc-lite - free, open source, twenty-plus years old - is all you need to talk to it.The programming model on the chip is usually JavaCard: a small applet, isolated by the card's runtime, selected by an application identifier (AID). The GlobalPlatform specifications cover how applets and keys get installed, updated, and retired on the card. If you have ever written an applet for a SIM, you have already written firmware for a secure element.And the host side is refreshingly small. Select the applet, exchange bytes:$ python collar_select.py ATR: 3B189657694C4C20200417 SELECT F000000001DEAD01 -> SW 6A82 follow-up INS 0x32 -> SW 6D00 That is the entire intimacy the host is allowed: eight bytes in, a MAC out, and the key stays inside a chip that was designed by paranoid people who assume lasers.For the record: this exchange is not a mock-up. While writing this article, the snippet above was executed against a generic CCID reader and an ordinary wallet card. ATR in, SELECT out, SW 6A82 back - "applet not found," exactly as designed; a follow-up command answered 6D00, "INS not supported." A card without the applet answers every command honestly - with status words, never with secrets. That is the entire thesis of this article, demonstrated in ninety seconds on hardware cheaper than lunch.And "assume lasers" is not a figure of speech. The attack catalogs behind secure element evaluations are public - they are the Common Criteria profiles - secure elements typically carry evaluations at EAL4+ or EAL5+ - and they read like a heist menu: simple and differential power analysis (watch the current, recover the key), electromagnetic emanation, voltage and clock glitching to make the chip skip the very instruction that checks your PIN, laser fault injection to flip individual bits, and microprobing: physically landing needles on the die. Against each of these the chip deploys countermeasures - randomized execution, dummy cycles, sensors that wipe state on anomaly. None of it is perfect; the game is cost asymmetry. A student can reproduce real DPA at home today with ChipWhisperer, an open-source side-channel platform that costs a few hundred dollars - which is exactly why shipping a bare software key in 2026 is not a risk decision, it is a gift.Inside the applet: the other side of the conversationThe host snippet shows half the conversation. Here is the other half - read it for its shape, not as an install-and-run recipe: a JavaCard applet, written fresh for this article on the public API, that MACs the host's INS 0x32 challenge with a key that exists only inside the chip. Where that key's value comes from is the very next section's question:Read both sides side by side and notice what is absent: the host code contains no key, and the applet code contains no key either - only a key object whose value arrives once, at personalization, through channels JavaCard isolates from the application. The secret exists in exactly one place on Earth, and no line of source code on either side of the conversation can print it. That is what "the key never leaves the chip" looks like when you spell it out in two languages.One version note before anyone runs this. needs Java Card 3.0.5 or newer, and most inexpensive developer cards still ship 2.2.2, where the call dies with a NO_SUCH_ALGORITHM exception - not because CMAC is exotic, but because the API you get depends on the card's runtime, not on your code. A card marked Java Card 3.0.5 Classic or newer (JCOP 4 and friends) understands this crypto suite as written; on an older card you would implement CMAC from plain AES primitives by hand - a fine exercise, and an early lesson in why the applet should treat the crypto suite as a parameter.The wire between: hosting the element on an MCUThe reader in the demo above exists because a desk and a PC are the fastest pipe to a card. Remove the reader and nothing about the conversation changes: the same APDUs travel over a bare ISO 7816-3 link, and the microcontroller speaks that link natively. This is the hardware level of the next collar revision - and the honest headline is that the pipe is hardware, the conversation is software, and only the pipe is new. A smart-card-package element needs VCC, GND, RST, and I/O; CLK is optional, because many elements clock themselves from an internal oscillator, and when a part does expect an external clock, an MCU timer covers it. Two of those wires are not wires at all, they are policy. VCC comes from a switchable rail so the element can be power-gated between sessions. RST goes to a GPIO, which buys a subtle field capability: you can bounce the secure element without rebooting the firmware that is logging the incident. I/O is half-duplex, one line, open-collector by convention - the whole link is closer to a doorbell wire than to a bus.The STM32 already speaks this dialect. The USART on an STM32L4 has a dedicated smartcard mode: half-duplex single-wire, 1.5 stop bits, a programmable guard time, and character timing derived from an ETU clock - the ISO 7816-3 framing, including parity-error signalling and the retransmission count, is hardware-assisted. T=0 character handling largely runs in silicon; T=1 block framing is a thin software layer on the same peripheral. What remains for firmware is small and boring, which is the compliment. In its shape, not a recipe - bit names live in the L4 reference manual:Note the order in : configuration registers refuse writes while the peripheral is enabled, so the full smartcard setup - CR2, the guard-time and prescaler in GTPR, and the CR3 mode switch - is programmed while UE is still zero; CR1 turns the USART on last. That is the same order ST's own HAL uses for smartcard init.A reset sequence, an ATR parse, an optional PPS negotiation to pick a faster bit rate, and that pump - a few hundred lines. No DMA glamour, no third-party stack required to say hello. The two loops at the bottom are the whole art of working with data on a T=0 card: the chip either says 61xx "there is more, ask politely", 6Cxx "you guessed the length wrong, ask again with this Le", or answers with a status word that is never a secret., in order: power the rail, de-assert RST, catch the ATR (the element's self-introduction - parse the interface bytes, note the historical bytes), optionally negotiate a faster ETU with a PPS, then SELECT the applet AID and wait for 90 00. From that moment the firmware is a client: it posts eight-byte challenges and receives MACs. Every later session repeats only the last two steps - the ATR ceremony is for boots and glitches, not for every message. One task owns the element. Other tasks post sign-requests to a queue and sleep; APDU streams never interleave, because interleaving is how you get two partial commands and a very confused chip. The MCU's persistent state is counters and session handles - nothing key-shaped ever lands in MCU flash, which is the entire point wearing an RTOS hat. The one genuinely dangerous moment in the whole life of the device is a brown-out during personalization: cutting power while a key write is in flight is how a one-dollar chip becomes a paperweight. Hence a deactivation sequence before every power cut and a supply rail that sags slower than the element's write time. Between sessions the element is power-gated to its leakage floor; waking it costs one ATR ceremony, a few milliseconds, done rarely. Per-message cost is unchanged - symmetric MAC, microseconds of CPU - because the radio, not the cryptography, remains the only budget that matters. The collar keeps its single-digit microamps in sleep; the secure element sleeps deeper than the dog.And the collar already carries one. The soldered eSIM on the tracker board is the same smart-card die in its smallest suit: an MFF2 package, five by six millimeters, hosting the carrier's applet, provisioned and rotated over the air by machinery the device never sees. The modem owns that link; the carrier owns the keys. That is the exact division of labor this article keeps arguing for - already shipped, working, on someone else's keys. The secure element adds a second die so that your keys, the ones your own backend depends on, live under the same discipline: born inside the chip, rotated over an authenticated channel, never readable by the device that uses them.And to keep the receipts straight: the host conversation above was executed on real hardware; the MCU link described here is public-spec wiring - ISO 7816-3 timing from the standard, smartcard mode from the STM32L4 reference manual, pin budgets from the element datasheets - into which that proven conversation drops unchanged. A standard interface is a promise that this sentence can be written: the pipe is new, the bytes are not.Here is the part that surprised me, and that I now believe is the actual difference between a demo and a product. The chip is the easy tenth.A key has a life: it is generated, injected, used, rotated, and eventually revoked. Each stage has failure modes that have nothing to do with cryptography: Somewhere between the assembly line and your desk, the device receives an identity. If that step happens over an uncontrolled interface, your supply chain is your attack surface. The first conversation between the device and your backend establishes trust. Do it badly - a shared transport key, a default PIN - and every later secret inherits the weakness. For the applet above, this ceremony is literally where the key object receives its value ( over the personalization APDU) - and only after that does mac.init(key, Signature.MODE_SIGN) become legal on a physical card. Keys should expire. To replace one you need a channel that is already authenticated... by a key. This chicken-and-egg problem has exactly two solutions: a second, longer-lived key, or a hardware root that signs the transition. One device falls off a truck. Now the backend must reject its identity without bricking the fleet, and the fleet must learn about the rejection without trusting the rejected device to relay it.None of these stages is visible in a demo. All of them are visible in year two of a deployment, usually at 2 a.m. When people say "secure element," this is what the phrase should call to mind: not a chip, but a pipeline that makes keys mortal and replaceable instead of immortal and exposed.The public world solved this pattern repeatedly. SIM cards do it for billions of devices - over-the-air key updates are a routine, specified operation. Bank cards rotate keys as a lifestyle. The constrained-IoT world mostly still ships one symmetric key per device per lifetime and calls it a day. That gap is where the next Mir comes from.The public cloud world has already industrialized the answer, and the patterns are documented openly. Claim-based, just-in-time provisioning: the device ships with a claim certificate, and its real identity is minted only at first boot, on the customer's network - AWS IoT documents this flow end to end. Azure Sphere did one better in spirit: a hardware root of trust feeding a security service that manages keys for the fleet's lifetime. Android's Verified Boot plus attestation is the same idea in your pocket: the chain from ROM to OS is measured, signed, and remotely provable. What these systems have in common is the direction of trust: the key does not exist before the device does, and nobody in the factory ever sees it in the clear. An IoT product of any size can copy this shape with one secure element per device and a backend that treats keys as inventory - born, rotated, retired - instead of constants compiled into a firmware image.Authentication on a microamp budgetThe collar sleeps at single-digit microamps. A full TLS handshake - certificates, asymmetric crypto, several round trips - keeps the radio and the CPU busy for seconds. On a battery meant to last years, seconds of radio are a budget line, and certificates are a size class the device cannot afford to store, parse, and verify. Public-key crypto is not free either: an ECDSA verification on a Cortex-M4 costs milliseconds-to-tens-of-milliseconds of full-tilt CPU, and in a device that measures its life in microamp-hours, that is a real entry in the ledger.Constrained networks answered this years ago, and their answers are worth copying: derives per-session keys from a long-term application key at every join, then authenticates each frame with a message integrity code and up/down frame counters. No certificates on the wire, ever. The public specification is readable in an evening, and so are the public post-mortems of deployments that shipped default keys or reset their counters - a complete education, positive and negative. does object security for CoAP: each message carries its own integrity protection and a sequence number, with a replay window on the receiving side. No session handshake per exchange; the pattern assumes a pre-established context. exists precisely for the "we need an authenticated key exchange, in bytes, on a device this size" case - a compact AKE designed to run before OSCORE, orders of magnitude lighter than a TLS handshake.The pattern underneath all three: one expensive handshake (or a factory-established key), then per-message integrity with counters and replay windows, in symmetric crypto, at a cost the battery can live with. If your protocol does not have frame counters and a replay window, it is not a constrained protocol; it is a wish.Here is the whole pattern as a running toy - both sides, public primitives only, no custom cryptography, just composition. The master key stands in for what the secure element holds; the receiver keeps a replay window:Run it and the third line prints the only verdict that matters: REJECTED: counter 41 already seen. That one line is the entire contribution of the replay window - and the reason a captured radio transcript is worthless.One more budget line belongs here, because devices outlive deployments. A collar shipped today will sit on a shelf, then on a dog, for ten to fifteen years. "Harvest now, decrypt later" is not a slogan when the harvest window is measured in decades; anyone recording today's traffic is buying a lottery ticket on future compute. The public answer, ML-KEM (FIPS 203), exists - but lattice key exchange on a Cortex-M4 costs real milliseconds and real RAM, and on a coin cell that is a genuine engineering dilemma, documented painfully in the public papers on constrained PQC. The honest current posture for a device this thin: symmetric authentication done right, AES-class session protection, and a hardware root - so that when the asymmetric migration is affordable, it is a firmware conversation, not a recall. Suite-agnostic by construction, again, buys the future.National suites are a fact of lifeOne more design property, cheap to get early and expensive to retrofit: the architecture should not care which cipher suites it runs. And "national suites" are not an exotic corner case - they are a standing fact of the industry. GOST, SM4, ARIA and SEED, Camellia: national cipher families from four different regulatory worlds, all with public English-language specifications and RFC coverage. If your device runs AES-GCM today and a regulator asks for one of these tomorrow, the request is not an attack on your architecture - it is a configuration change. If it is anything more than a configuration change, the architecture is the bug.The GOST family makes a good public case study precisely because its paper trail is long and open. It starts with a Soviet-era block cipher, GOST 28147-89, declassified in the nineties and later carried into English-language RFCs. The modern standard, GOST R 34.12-2015, defines two ciphers in one document: Magma, the 64-bit-block successor of the old cipher, and Kuznyechik, a 128-bit-block design for the new era. Modes of operation live in GOST R 34.13-2015; the Streebog hash function in GOST R 34.11-2012. Every one of these has an English RFC you can read tonight: the cipher usages, the TLS suites, the hash - and, my favorite for this article's theme, a public RFC for re-keying: regular session-key renewal as a formalized protocol operation, exactly the lifecycle discipline the previous section keeps begging for.The Kuznyechik story also carries the article's thesis in one anecdote. In 2019, an academic researcher published an analysis of its S-box and found a hidden mathematical structure - a compact algorithmic description of a table the standard presents as arbitrary constants [2]. Thirty years of standardization, and the true generator of the table surfaced not from the designers but from outside cryptanalysis. Whatever one believes about how that structure got there, the engineering lesson survives every interpretation: secret by design is fragile by design. A construction whose security story depends on undocumented choices will eventually meet someone who reads structure into the noise - which is, again, the argument for public primitives with public scrutiny, and against homebrew.What concretely changes when a suite changes: block size (64 vs 128 bits changes how you pack counters and nonces), MAC construction and length, key sizes, and the performance profile on your MCU. Which is why the applet should accept the suite as a parameter, not as a personality - and why the backend ledger records it per device per epoch. When a migration request arrives, "suite-agnostic by construction" is the difference between a firmware update and a product recall.The regulation is already hereIf the engineering argument is not enough: the legal one arrived. sets baseline security provisions for consumer IoT - no universal default passwords, a means to manage credentials, secure storage, secure updates - and it has stopped being a suggestion. The UK's Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure act has been in force since April 2024, banning default passwords on consumer connectables [3]. The EU followed harder: under the Radio Equipment Directive's delegated act, cybersecurity requirements for connected devices became mandatory from August 2025, with the EN 18031 series as the harmonized route [4]. The US Cyber Trust Mark is building the same pressure from the labeling side.Read that list again and notice something: no universal default passwords, secure storage, updatable credentials. That is not a compliance document - that is the checklist below, wearing a lanyard. The eight questions at the end of this article stopped being hygiene advice somewhere in the last two years; they are now the shape of market access. A device that cannot answer them is not merely insecure. It is unsellable in a growing share of the map, and the share is growing.Taped above my desk since the evening I re-read my own provisioning code. Eight questions before any device speaks to the internet:Where was the key born, and who else was in the room?Can the device output its own key? (The only correct answer is no, by hardware.)What authenticates the first message after power-on?Where do frame counters live, and what happens on reset or overflow?How does a key get replaced - over what channel, signed by whom?One device is stolen. Name the exact steps to revoke it and the maximum time the backend keeps trusting it.Which debug interfaces are open in the shipped firmware, and what does opening each one cost the attacker?What does the device do when the backend says "I no longer believe you"?If any answer starts with "we should probably," that is a no.The next hardware revision of the collar is already designed differently, and the difference is not a bigger microcontroller. It is a secure element beside the MCU, keys that have never touched firmware, message counters with a replay window, and a provisioning pipeline I would be comfortable demonstrating to a hostile audience - because the secrets involved are, by construction, not present anywhere I could accidentally show them.The dog still does not care. The battery budget still comes first. But the collar is now a device whose keys can be revoked, rotated, and audited, and the door no longer has the combination hanging beside it.The earlier chapter of this story - the firmware and OTA side - is . An independent teardown of the collar's firmware methods, published by WeSpeakIoT, is .The lock is not the product. The lifecycle is. - the application protocol data unit: one command-reply exchange with the card, ending in two status bytes. - answer to reset: the card's self-introduction on power-up, including its name and preferred protocols. - application identifier: the address by which a host selects one applet among many on a card. - a tamper-resistant chip holding keys that cannot be commanded out. - the two classic smart card transmission protocols; T=0 is byte-oriented, T=1 block-oriented. - a subset-of-Java runtime for smart cards; applets are selected by AID and speak APDU. - the one-time injection of identity and keys into a device or card. - message integrity code: a MAC over (counter, payload) that makes tampering and replay visible. - a monotonic per-message number; the backbone of replay protection. - the receiver's bookkeeping of seen counters; below or inside it, messages die. - RFC 5869 key derivation: turning one long-term secret into per-purpose session keys. - a soldered smart-card package, 5 x 6 mm; the same die as a SIM or a bank card, dressed for a PCB. - the wallet-card form factor: 85.6 x 53.98 mm of plastic with a contact pad. - the public evaluation framework and its assurance levels; SE chips typically ship at EAL4+.References & further reading

item.title: Math Professor Accuses OpenAI of Copying His Work, Says AI Compute Power Makes Racing to Publish 'Pointless'
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
The New York Post wrote that OpenAI "stunned the mathematics world" last week when it announced its AI model "cracked a legendary math problem left unsolved for nearly a century in just 88 hours."
But a New York University professor "has come forward alleging OpenAI may have copied his work after asking him to collaborate — with one of the company's scientists allegedly warning he might 'ruin his career' if he refused."
[P]rofessor Tristan Buckmaster, a British-Australian researcher who trained in Germany... had been working with Long Island-raised math prodigy Levent Alpöge, a researcher with OpenAI rival Anthropic, on a different elusive fluid dynamics equation, known as the Euler problem, when he found a solution using AI tools from both Anthropic and ChatGPT. He said scientists from OpenAI approached him and tried to convince him to jointly announce the solution, claiming they had independently solved Navier-Stokes. Buckmaster questioned the timing of their finding the solution in a blog post, noting OpenAI had only done so "in the past few days" — after the company became aware of his work. He asked OpenAI experts whether its AI systems used to solve the equation had been "trained on, or had access to" his research, but said they declined to answer, prompting him to wonder how they had advanced toward the solution so quickly. The puzzle is "not the direction one arrives at in a few days," Buckmaster wrote incredulously...
In OpenAI's post on its website sharing the Navier-Stokes proof, which it credited to Astra, the company's latest AI bot, the firm insisted no user data was incorporated into its model to solve the problem. However, it noted that it "cannot rule out" that anonymized data was used to "improve our models."
"We congratulate Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster on their remarkable mathematical work," OpenAI said in the announcement.
Buckmaster shot back, "Is it ethical to use customer's data to try to scoop their customer?"
Alpöge's affiliation with Anthropic "seems to have been a sore point for OpenAI," writes TechCrunch.
Buckmaster's public statement says the OpenAI's Sebastien "twice asserted that he wanted Levent removed from authorship" and also said that "it was so annoying that Levent works at Anthropic" — but that Buckmaster still refused to remove the Anthropic mathematician's credit.
I said that if OpenAI released its result in the way proposed I would go public with what happened. The reply was, "Why would you ruin your career?" [OpenAI's Bubeck said later on X that he'd meant unfounded accusations could damage Buckmaster's career.] I replied that I am an academic, and asked why he thought going public would ruin my career. The reply was, "If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice."
Buckmaster later told Australia's public broadcaster ABC that the companies building AI "have zero respect for the scientific community. I mean, it's appalling, honestly." But he went on to say AI has made the race to publish mathematical breakthroughs pointless.
"I think it's pointless. Like, I think the game is up...." Professor Buckmaster said he and Dr Alpöge had more research they could publish but questioned the point of racing ahead with it when AI could perform work that had previously occupied researchers for years.
He said there needed to be a discussion about how mathematics should operate in this new environment. Professor Buckmaster said some mathematicians had stopped publicly sharing what they were working on to avoid tipping off AI companies about their plans. He has called on academics and people from OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepMind to discuss ground rules for how they worked together. He said the companies' power carried responsibilities that went beyond competing to solve problems before their rivals...
Building on the work of mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, the pair found a solution to the Euler problem, a stepping stone to the Navier-Stokes problem. Professor Buckmaster said he spent weeks checking and improving the "slop" proofs generated by AI...
For now, Professor Buckmaster said he wanted to finish existing work and support his PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, rather than chase another Millennium Prize. "I think it's more important to re-evaluate what math is," he said.
"The New York University professor also warned Australia about the centralisation of resources into the hands of a small number of privately owned foreign companies..."

item.title: How to audit what your AI agents are accessing
item.author: ameliepangolin
item.content:encoded: Have you ever asked an LLM in chat what seemed like a simple question, then watched as it reinvented fire, the wheel, and quantum physics to tell you how far Scotiabank Arena is from the Toronto airport?AI agents, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and OpenClaw, can do that, too. But their users explicitly encourage them to dig deep. Agents can make dozens of LLM requests per task, invoke tools, and pass data to one or more providers. So who sent what data to which model, and where is it logged?If you’re using Aperture, you can see, store, and control access to this data.Here’s how Aperture works to help you audit what your AI agents are accessing, who’s managing them, and where it’s all logged.Every AI request has an identity attachedAperture’s ability to rein in AI agent sprawl starts with its identity layer. Every request routed through Aperture comes with cryptographic proof of identity through Tailscale. When tokens are set on fire, you’ll know where the smoke started.Every time a person or a agent makes a request through Aperture, their login name, device ID, and any related tags are pulled from their identity. The same goes for tagged “non-human” devices, like CI runners or background agents, which pick up an identity from their tags.You don’t have to go message-by-message through a coding session or chat session, thanks to Aperture’s session tracking. Related requests are all grouped into sessions, so you can see the context of the data, tools, and costs associated with deeper work.Identity flows through the whole system: every record, dashboard, and session log. You can always answer “Who did this,” and the answer is a specific person or device. Some vendors try to provide visibility by pulling every user, and every job, into a single ecosystem and control panel. Aperture provides consistent identity, visibility, and control layers across whatever tools teams choose to use.What data is captured, where it’s keptAperture captures the full request-response lifecycle of every LLM interaction. Administrators get granular access and control to what data is being retained and where it ends up.Here’s what Aperture captures:The full request body from a userFull response body from the LLMHTTP headers (with sensitive values redacted)Token counts by type (input/output/cached/reasoning)All of this is captured asynchronously, after a response is completed. Aperture doesn’t slow down AI work in any way.How much captured data you want to keep is up to you. You can reduce your capture log retention all the way down to zero. You can export logs to S3-compatible storage for your SIEM system so you can detect and respond to threats. Or you could do both, holding no data, but still having a full audit trail.You can let trusted partners into your data, too. Aperture has already built APIs and integrations with Cribl, Oso, Apollo Research, and Cerbos, with more to come.Who can see the logs (and who can’t)Aperture’s access policy for session data is deny-by-default. Access to logs, just like access to models, is controlled through a grants system, one that can map directly onto Tailscale identities.Grants can be highly specific (), categorical (), or open-door (). In Aperture, you can also scope by provider and model, like or , and set MCP tool access through grants, too. There are two roles at the moment, user and admin, with more to come soon.If you’ve already got Tailscale grants configured, you can set up Aperture in the same tailnet policy. Aperture and Tailscale grants combine additively.Administrator access loggingAlong with insights into AI use, Aperture, unlike most gateways, can also log what administrators do with those logs.When someone with an admin role views logs owned by another user, the access is recorded. Other administrators can review the audit trail, either by API endpoint or Aperture’s web interface. It’s a clear signal to auditors that admin access to sensitive session data is both tracked and reviewable.Enforcing policy before data leaves your networkAperture’s policies wouldn’t mean much if all you could do is see what went out the door. By providing LLM access through Aperture, policies can be enforced requests hit their providers, through guardrails. You can see not only what did happen, but what was blocked from happening.Pre-request hooks can scrub personally identifiable information (PII), block requests that violate data policy, or strip out specific tool declarationsShould the guardrail service be unreachable, requests can be configured to fail_closed (blocked) or fail_open (proceed)Aperture partners can add fine-grained authorization at the tool-call level, allowing or denying individual callsQuotas can enforce spending per user, group, agent, or run, across all providers.Auditing highly active AI agents requires identity, logging, and visibility into who can see what. Smart limits on data, tools, and spending are a natural outgrowth of Aperture’s gateway design. It’s a single place to see what’s happening, what happened, and what's being blocked from happening with your LLM tools.See for yourself by getting started with Aperture on any Tailscale account, including our Personal plan. If you’d like to know more about how Aperture would fit your organization’s needs, contact us and we’ll walk you through it.

item.title: Why Remote Teams Still Struggle to Build Trust, Even When the Meetings Go Fine
item.author: Jon Stojan Journalist
item.content:encoded: Most engineering orgs will tell you their remote tooling works. Standups happen. Documentation gets written. Decisions get made and recorded somewhere searchable. And yet trust between teams that rarely interact keeps eroding anyway, in a way nobody can quite trace back to a specific broken process, because the process is not what broke.A thought leader who examines disconnection for a living has a theory for why that gap is so hard to name. Edward Garcia spent years applying it to cities and public health systems before turning it toward distributed teams specifically. His starting point is that an office was never only a workspace. It doubled as something closer to plumbing: mostly invisible, quietly responsible for a lot more than anyone gave it credit for.Garcia's diagnosis is specific rather than nostalgic. Companies that went remote did the obvious part of the job well. Meetings moved to video calls. Memos became shared documents. Hallway conversations became Slack threads. What never got rebuilt, in his view, is the layer sitting underneath all of that: the unplanned interaction that used to happen without anyone scheduling it, a new hire absorbing how senior engineers actually work by watching them, someone overhearing a conversation that turns out to be relevant to a problem they are stuck on.The practical effect, in his read, is that distributed teams get very good at one kind of connection and steadily worse at another. People who already know they need to talk to each other can do so instantly, from anywhere. People who do not yet know they have a reason to talk almost never find that out by accident anymore, because accident was doing more work than anyone realized.Independent research backs the pattern. A , based on six months of data from more than 61,000 Microsoft employees, found that firm-wide remote work caused collaboration networks to become more static and siloed, with fewer bridges between parts of the organization that did not already work closely together, alongside a broader shift from synchronous toward asynchronous communication.Garcia heads off the obvious response before it lands. Ordering people back into an office does not fix this on its own, because sitting in the same building was never actually the mechanism. A team can be fully in person five days a week and still barely know each other outside their immediate group. What mattered was never the room. It was the conditions the room happened to create without anyone designing them on purpose.He calls the discipline of recreating those conditions deliberately Social Connection Architecture, a framework he developed through his work co-founding the . Applied to a distributed team, the idea is to stop asking how to make remote work feel like an office and start asking what specific relational functions the office used to perform, then design deliberately for those functions instead.In practice, Garcia's prescription is smaller than most remote culture initiatives, and less frequent than people expect. Not a retreat. Not a virtual happy hour, which he considers an occasional event rather than something that reliably builds trust over time. His preferred fix is short, repeated conversations between people who have no immediate work reason to talk, engineers from different teams paired for twenty minutes every few weeks, with nothing required to come out of it. The point is not the conversation itself. It is getting close to what used to happen by running into the same person often enough to actually know them.“If every conversation has an agenda, deliverable, facilitator, and performance objective, you have simply created another meeting,” Garcia said. Strip the productivity requirement away, in his framing, or the exercise stops functioning as the thing it was meant to rebuild.He is equally specific about what shared time in person should be used for once a team does travel to be together. Two days of conference room presentations people could have watched from their desks wastes the one resource distributed teams cannot get back easily. Garcia argues that scarce in-person time works better spent on mentoring, difficult conversations, and the kind of problem solving that genuinely benefits from being in a room, rather than the parts of work that already function fine on a screen.“The lesson from remote work is not that connection requires an office,” Garcia said. “It is that connection requires infrastructure.” The office supplied that infrastructure so quietly that almost nobody registered it as infrastructure while it was still there. Its absence has been just as easy to miss, which is exactly why it keeps costing companies more than most of them have noticed.This story was distributed as a release by Jon Stojan under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging Program.

item.title: A Developer's Guide to Database Architecture and Performance Fundamentals
item.author: Syed Ahmer Shah
item.content:encoded:
When your application needs to find a customer record among millions of entries, seconds matter. But the real mystery isn't the speed—it's how databases manage to locate one specific record from billions in milliseconds. This guide unravels that mystery by examining the core machinery that powers modern data systems.Most developers treat databases as black boxes. You send queries in; data comes back. But that simplistic view breaks down the moment performance matters.The Problem With Unstructured DataConsider building an e-commerce platform from scratch. You could theoretically store everything in flat files—CSVs, JSON, even raw text files. Many startups do exactly this initially. Then reality hits: Your application now serves 500 concurrent users. Two customers simultaneously purchase your last inventory item. Your system crashes mid-transaction, corrupting financial records. Your Excel export contains 50GB of redundant customer information copied across thousands of rows.These aren't hypothetical problems—they're the exact issues that led to database management systems in the first place.The Two Database PhilosophiesThe database world has split into two camps, each solving different problems: (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server) enforce rigid structure. Your data must fit predefined columns and types. This strictness prevents chaos and enables powerful guarantees about data integrity.Document-Oriented Systems (MongoDB, Firestore) embrace flexibility. Store objects however you want. No schema enforcement. The trade-off? You lose some safety guarantees.Neither approach is universally superior. PostgreSQL excels when your data relationships matter. MongoDB shines when your schema evolves constantly.Before writing a single query, you need a blueprint. This is where most mistakes happen.Your data doesn't exist in isolation. In that e-commerce system:Customers generate OrdersOrders reference ProductsProducts exist in CategoriesCategories contain SubcategoriesThese connections aren't accidental—they're the structure of your domain. Missing a relationship means writing complex, inefficient queries later. Modeling relationships poorly means data corruption at scale. (primary keys) ensure each record is distinct. (foreign keys) connect tables. This creates a web of relationships that mirrors your actual business logic.Some relationships are straightforward: one customer, many orders. Others are complex: many students in many courses (many-to-many). Handling these properly requires that bridge the gap.Here's a common mistake: storing everything in one massive table. Customer name, address, email appear alongside order dates, product prices, and inventory counts. A customer with 100 orders means their information is duplicated 100 times.This creates cascading problems:Update a customer's email? Now you need to update 100 rows.Delete an order? Risk corrupting customer data if you're not careful.Storage balloons unnecessarily. solves this by separating concerns. Customer data lives in its own table. Orders reference customers via keys. Each piece of information exists in exactly one place.However, modern practice acknowledges a counterintuitive truth: sometimes redundancy is the right answer. If you constantly query customer names alongside orders, splitting these across tables forces expensive join operations. Strategically duplicating data can actually improve performance.The real skill is knowing when to normalize and when to denormalize. Pure theory yields poor systems. So does ignoring structure entirely.The Language Layer: SQL and BeyondSchema design is meaningless without a way to interact with it. SQL fills that role across nearly all structured databases.The Four Fundamental OperationsEvery database interaction reduces to four primitives:INSERT → Store new records SELECT → Retrieve existing records UPDATE → Modify records in place DELETE → Remove records permanently These operations (CRUD) are literally all you need to build any database application. Everything else is optimization.Here's where SQL transitions from simple to powerful. You have customers in one table and orders in another. To answer "show me each customer and their recent purchases," you need to these tables:SELECT c.name, o.purchase_date, o.total_amount FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.purchase_date > '2024-01-01' The JOIN operation is where relational databases prove their worth. Different join strategies answer different questions:: Only customers with orders: All customers, including those without orders: All orders, with customer data where available: Everything from both tablesRaw data isn't insight. You need to it:SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) as purchase_count, SUM(o.total_amount) as lifetime_value FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 This groups orders by customer and applies calculations. Which customers matter most? This query tells you.Theory breaks down at scale. With 500 million customer records, a search without proper indexing becomes unusably slow.How Indexing Changes the GameImagine finding a name in a phone book. Scanning every entry sequentially would take hours. But phone books exist precisely because they're alphabetically indexed. You jump directly to the right section.Database indexes work identically. When you search by email, an index maps email addresses to their storage locations. Instead of scanning 500 million records, the database navigates a data structure (typically a B-tree) that narrows the search space exponentially.The impact is staggering: finding a specific record drops from seconds (or minutes) to microseconds.But indexes aren't free of charge:: Every index duplicates data in a different structure.: Inserting a customer now requires updating the name index, email index, phone index, etc.: Indexes consume RAM, reducing space for caching actual data.This is why you don't index every column. Strategic indexing on columns used in WHERE clauses and JOIN conditions yields massive returns. Over-indexing degrades performance.Understanding Query PlansWhen you execute a query, the database doesn't necessarily execute it the way you wrote it. A sophisticated component called the considers alternatives and picks the fastest approach.EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email = 'john@example.com' This reveals the database's plan: whether it's using your email index (good) or scanning the entire table (bad). Slow query? The query plan is where investigation starts.Reliability Layer: Transactions and Data SafetyHere's why databases exist beyond raw storage: safety guarantees.The Money Transfer ScenarioImagine implementing a payment system. Account A sends $500 to Account B:Deduct $500 from Account AWhat if step 1 completes, then the server crashes before step 2? Money vanishes from Account A but never appears in Account B. Your financial records are corrupted. prevent this by bundling steps into atomic units: either both complete, or neither does. Partial success is impossible.ACID: The Database GuaranteeThis safety is formalized in four principles:: Changes complete entirely or not at all.: The database maintains valid rules (balances never go negative, foreign keys always exist, etc.).: Concurrent transactions don't interfere. One user's transaction doesn't see another's in-progress changes.: Once saved, data survives hardware failures.Most SQL databases provide these guarantees by default. Most NoSQL databases require careful configuration to achieve them.Concurrency and Conflict ResolutionMultiple users modifying data simultaneously creates conflicts. Two customers buying the last item. Two transfers from the same account. How does the database prevent double-selling? is the simplest approach: hold exclusive access to a record while modifying it. Other transactions wait their turn. Simple but can create (Transaction A waits for B, B waits for A). Modern databases detect and break deadlocks automatically.More sophisticated approaches like (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) let readers and writers coexist by maintaining multiple versions of data. PostgreSQL and Oracle use this approach to achieve better concurrency.Academic knowledge and production systems diverge sharply here.Here's a seemingly innocent pattern:# Fetch all customers customers = db.query("SELECT * FROM customers")
# For each customer, fetch their orders for customer in customers: orders = db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", customer.id) # Process orders... With 1,000 customers, this executes 1,001 queries. The naive approach cascades into disaster.: Fetch all orders for all customers in a single query, then match them in application logic.: Combine both operations: one query with a JOIN instead of 1,001 queries.Query optimization libraries: Many frameworks provide tools to automatically prevent N+1 patterns.Connection Pooling and Resource ManagementEach database connection carries overhead. Opening 1,000 connections to handle 1,000 users burns memory and CPU. maintains a small pool of reusable connections. Applications check out connections, use them, and return them. Multiple users share the same physical connections.This technique alone can improve throughput by an order of magnitude.Displaying 1,000,000 results on a single page is nonsensical. Pagination breaks results into manageable chunks. But approaches differ: () skips the first 200 rows to fetch the next 10. Simple to understand but increasingly slow with large offsets—the database still counts and discards those 200 rows. uses the last row's values to fetch subsequent pages. Faster at scale and prevents duplicate results if data changes between requests, but requires sorted, unique identifiers.Your schema isn't permanent. As products evolve, you add columns, remove fields, or restructure tables. are versioned scripts that safely transform schemas without data loss.Poor migrations corrupt data. Good migrations run predictably and can be rolled back if problems arise.Querying the database repeatedly for identical data is wasteful. Application-level caching (using Redis, Memcached) stores frequently accessed data in memory. The application checks the cache first, hitting the database only on misses.Caching introduces complexity—stale data, cache invalidation, consistency challenges—but at scale, it's essential for performance.Database Selection: Making the Right ChoiceDifferent databases excel at different problems. The choice depends on your specific needs. offers an exceptional combination of features, reliability, and performance. Full ACID compliance, complex queries, advanced indexing strategies, and even JSON support. For most applications, PostgreSQL is the default choice. prioritizes simplicity and speed. It's lighter weight than PostgreSQL and handles straightforward queries efficiently. Perfect for web applications where complexity is limited. brings enterprise-grade features and tight Windows integration. Common in corporate environments with established Microsoft infrastructure. stores JSON-like documents instead of rows. Eliminates schema enforcement, allowing flexibility. Useful for applications with evolving or unstructured data. The trade-off: weaker consistency guarantees and different query patterns. is Google's managed NoSQL offering. Serverless, auto-scaling, and globally distributed. Ideal for mobile and web applications where infrastructure management isn't your focus.Structured data with defined relationships? SQL.Complex queries and strict consistency requirements? SQL.Rapidly evolving schema? NoSQL.Primarily key-value lookups? Consider NoSQL or specialized key-value stores.Need automatic geographic replication? Cloud NoSQL.Building in a startup with limited ops resources? Managed services (Firestore, DynamoDB).A database is ultimately a disciplined compromise between convenience and safety. It trades raw simplicity for structure. It sacrifices write speed for read reliability. It enforces rules that prevent corruption while enabling fast queries.The complexity you encounter in production databases—transactions, indexes, query planning, locking protocols—isn't accidental overengineering. Each piece solves real problems that emerge at scale. The best engineers understand not just how to use databases, but why they work the way they do.Moving From Understanding to MasteryThis foundation covers the essential concepts. But mastery requires deeper exploration: understanding B-tree structures, transaction isolation levels, query optimization techniques, and distributed database challenges.Start with PostgreSQL on a real project. Make your schema choices thoughtfully. Write clear queries and monitor their performance. Learn to read query plans. Understand your bottlenecks before optimizing.The database skills you build now will serve you across decades and countless projects.

item.title: ChatGPT-Using Lawyer Cited Its Fake Witnesses and Police Testimony in Court
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Reuters reports:
A defense lawyer appealing his client's murder conviction submitted a brief containing made-up police testimony and witnesses fabricated by OpenAI's ChatGPT, New Mexico's highest court said. The New Mexico Supreme Court on Wednesday fined the attorney, Stephen Aarons [for $5,000], and held him in contempt for failing to verify the accuracy of the court filing, which Aarons said he prepared with help from the AI program... and said they will refer him to an attorney disciplinary board for investigation.
Aarons in a statement to Reuters said he had used ChatGPT to summarize the trial proceedings when he agreed to take up the defendant's appeal last year, and did not understand the degree to which AI could "hallucinate" facts. "I am remorseful but hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake," he said.... Dozens of lawyers have been sanctioned for filing briefs where AI made up case citations or misquoted the law. Aarons' filing appears to have gone further, containing fabricated witness testimony in a criminal appeal...
Aarons told the court at an August 21 hearing that he fed a computer-generated transcript and other case materials to ChatGPT, presuming it would generate "a bulletproof summary." The justices sounded incredulous that Aarons was not fully aware of how AI can make mistakes. "Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what's going on in the world?" Justice C. Shannon Bacon said at the hearing. "Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an above-the-fold story every single day."
"OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment."

item.title: Agentic Growth Hacking: What It Is and Why the Next Decade of Distribution Belongs to It
item.author: Nica Furs
item.content:encoded: Growth hacking was a human discipline: a small team found a behavior a platform rewarded, exploited it before anyone else noticed, and moved on when the platform closed the gap. It worked because platforms were young and humans were faster than the platforms' ability to patch. Both conditions are gone. Platforms are mature, their ranking systems are retrained continuously, and no human team can run hypotheses faster than the systems drift.Agentic growth hacking is what replaces it. The definition: the continuous, autonomous discovery of how distribution platforms decide what gets seen, and the governed execution of that knowledge on behalf of a brand, at machine speed, across every platform at once.enso coined the term and runs the only lab built entirely around it. What follows is how the discipline works, why it has to be structured the way it is, and why it succeeds in both growth hacking and inbound marketing.A distribution platform is a decision system (e.g. an algorithm). Somewhere inside it is a ranking model, a trust model, a moderation model and a citation model, each trained on signals you cannot see, each deciding whether a post travels, a comment survives, a source is trusted, a page is quoted, a message is delivered. Those models are the real product. Your content is a feature vector they score.Traditional marketing treats the platform as an audience and optimizes the input. Agentic growth hacking treats the platform as a black box and performs system identification on it: infer the transfer function from inputs to outcomes by controlled perturbation. The posture is borrowed from security research and from experimental science rather than from advertising. Define a scope. State a hypothesis about how the system responds to a specific input. Run it against a control. Measure a delta. Document it. Assume the finding has a half-life, because the box is being retrained while you study it.That posture implies two design constraints. Learning must be continuous, because the target is non-stationary. And learning must be separated from acting, because an optimizer that is free to discover what works will also discover what violates the platform's terms. That is not a hypothetical. It is reward hacking, and it is the default failure mode of any autonomous system pointed at a metric.The architecture: two layers, one gate, one ledgerEvery agentic growth system worth the name separates into a learning layer and an execution layer, with a controlled boundary between them and a shared record underneath. is autonomous and exploratory (mostly using frameworks like Hermes and OpenClaw). It observes platform signals, forms hypotheses about the ranking policy, proposes actions, and improves from outcomes. Architecturally this is a self-improving agent runtime: a long-running process with layered memory (session history, searchable episodic memory, operator profile, and procedural memory that is front-loaded into context), trajectory mining that extracts reusable patterns from its own past runs, and skill synthesis that writes those patterns down as versioned, loadable instruction files. The learner manages the exploration-exploitation trade-off explicitly, treating candidate policies as arms of a bandit and allocating experiments toward the ones with the highest expected information gain, not just the highest current lift.Reward shaping is the most important decision in this layer. The learner optimizes whatever it is rewarded on. Reward engagement and it learns to bait engagement. Reward durable metrics, survival of an action over time, lift against a control, downstream demand attributable to the action, and it learns what the platform actually values. Goodhart's law is not a warning here; it is the design spec.The learning layer holds no credentials. It operates under least privilege inside a sandbox with read access to the ledger and compute, and a deny-list that covers every tool capable of touching a platform. It reads outcomes. It proposes. It never acts. is deterministic and auditable. It performs actions on platforms, and it does so as workflows, not conversations. Two kinds:Scripted workflows have no model in the loop. They are event-driven and idempotent: triggers, timers, jittered schedules, rate limits, allow-lists, retries with backoff, structured logging. Anything with no decision inside it runs here.Agentic workflows are a fixed directed graph in which specific nodes call a model for a bounded task, such as classification, grounded generation, or intent scoring, and every irreversible edge passes through a human-in-the-loop gate. The graph is static. Only node contents are generated. Guardrails are properties of the graph, not sentences in a prompt: a prompt that forbids an action is a request, a graph with no node for that action is a fact.Per-entity state machines live here too. Each account, prospect or thread carries a state, transitions are guarded by conditions evaluated on a fixed cadence, and no action fires unless its guard is true. Guards are calibrated per segment and per locale, because the same observable signal has different false-positive rates in different contexts. is human and versioned (say, human-in-the-loop): The learning layer writes policies as skill files into a draft namespace. A reviewer promotes them against a fixed checklist: is there a control group or holdout, is the reward a durable metric, does the action set fit an existing workflow graph, what is the abort condition, what is the re-test interval. Only promoted skills load into execution. Draft and active namespaces are separate on disk, and the executor cannot read drafts. It is not sophisticated. It is the entire safety model, and its simplicity is the point. is append-only. Every observation, every action, every approval, every outcome against its control, with timestamps. It is simultaneously the training signal for the learning layer, the audit trail for the execution layer, the source of truth for attribution and credit assignment, and the evidence that gets published.Run continuously, the system is a research program, not a campaign. Sub-agents sample each platform's observable signals on a schedule, plus inferred ones: velocity curves, survival status, citation state, answer-engine snapshots for target queries, diffed over time. Everything lands in the ledger. The learner reads outcomes, runs analysis in its sandbox, and proposes a policy with a verification plan attached. A reviewer promotes or rejects the policy. Workflows act inside their limits, with approvals on irreversible edges. Outcomes are measured against controls using robust statistics, medians over means on heavy-tailed distributions, and durable metrics over engagement metrics. Findings enter the record, including nulls and failures, so the published wins stay honest. Every policy carries a half-life and a re-test schedule. A drift monitor watches lift decay in the ledger; when a policy falls below its threshold, it is retired and archived, not quietly left running.Step seven is what separates the discipline from a bag of tricks. A growth hack is a finding with a decay curve. The asset is not the finding. The asset is the rate at which the system finds the next one relative to the rate at which platforms close the last one. That ratio is the only metric that compounds.Why this succeeds inboundInbound assumed a human would read the content and a search engine would route them to it. Both assumptions are failing. Buyers ask a model; the model reads on their behalf; the model performs its own retrieval and decides which source to cite. Search is becoming generative, and visibility inside a generated answer is governed by citation graphs, entity authority and source trust rather than by keyword rank. Meanwhile paid acquisition has become a tax rather than a strategy, because the barrier to shipping a product has collapsed and every competitor bids on the same top-of-funnel intent.Distribution is moving off the auction and away from the reader, toward the layer where ranking policies, trust signals and citation behavior decide who exists to a buyer. That layer cannot be bought and cannot be written for. It can only be learned. Agentic growth hacking is the discipline of learning it, and the first go-to-market model designed for an audience that is partly machine.Learning the policies of many platforms, governing execution across them, and proving results against controls is research. It needs an environment where experiments are scoped, run, verified and published, and where the accumulating record is the product.That is why enso is built as an agentic growth lab rather than a software vendor. The lab operates agents on behalf of companies inside the platforms where their buyers are, runs each engagement as a scoped experimental program, and publishes what it learns, including the failures. The published record does three things at once: it holds the lab to a standard of evidence the industry has never had, it compounds into a map of how the largest distribution systems make decisions, and it teaches the discipline to anyone who reads it.The method is open. enso maintains the reference skills for the discipline as open source, in the same loadable instruction format the learning layer writes, so the playbooks travel even where the service does not. Categories belong to whoever writes the canonical practice, and this one is being written in public.The idea is not automation of spam. A learner that can discover what works will discover vote manipulation, sockpuppets and mass-following. Every one of those is reward hacking with a ban attached. The two-layer architecture exists so the learner never holds the tools that make them possible, and the durable-metric reward exists so it is never incentivized to want them. It is not a substitute for substance. The platforms' trust and moderation models reward grounded value more reliably than any tactic, and survival-based metrics cannot be gamed for long. Agentic growth hacking finds the rules. It does not manufacture the thing being distributed.It is not a tactic, because tactics expire. This is an operating model for a marketing and distribution functions in which the platforms are systems under study, the agents are researchers, the humans are reviewers, and the evidence is public.

item.title: What Morrowind Can Teach Us About Learning New Skills
item.author: Radu
item.content:encoded: All heroes and villains have an origin story. So why shouldn’t apps have as well? and its underlying philosophy are the product of countless hours of playing, sorry, I meant studying one of the masterpieces of the 21st century: the third video game in the Elder Scrolls series, .In case you haven't had the privilege of playing it, Morrowind is basically Skyrim's weird, xenophobic cousin.Our story will be told through the eyes of my in-game character, Cedric the Persistent.Cedric can't swing a sword without hurting himself and he can't cast even the most basic of spells. He's weak, poor, and probably illiterate. He's got the charm of a brick wall.But what do a 20 year old video game and our hopeless hero have to do with learning new skills? Well, Morrowind, by design or by accident, has one of the best models of skill acquisition in any video game. It's the closest match to how you get better at casting spells in real life.Let me briefly explain how it works. Let's take Cedric here for example. He's not the brightest tool in the shed, but he has a burning desire to become the best wizard there is.So, what does he do? He goes to the local shop and buys a tome that promises to teach him how to cast a huge, beautiful Fireball. It takes some time for Cedric to understand the tome. He can barely read after all. But eventually he thinks he's got a good enough understanding of the spell to try it out.He focuses intently and attempts to cast the spell and ....... nothing happens. He tries again and guess what? Nothing happens.Cedric is devastated, his sole dream seems impossible right now. How will he become the greatest wizard in the realm if he can't even cast a simple fireball? The locals are relieved however and put down the water buckets. Having your house burn down because of some over-ambitious wannabe wizard ain't fun.Cedric went in over his head. His skill level in casting spells is only 20 out of 100. In non geek terms, it means he's an idiot for even attempting to cast such a complex spell.Any normal person would think that maybe wizardry isn't for them, but not Cedric. He is called the Persistent after all. He is not prepared to abandon his dreams of fame, glory and riches as Morrowind's top wizard. The next day he returns to the shop and he buys another spell tome, this time for a much easier spell. A spell that creates a tiny spark.Eager to try it out, he walks to the middle of the town and prepares to cast it. The townspeople panic and prepare their buckets again. Cedric focuses all his attention, makes the magic hand gestures and this time the tiniest spark emerges from the tip of his index finger.He is overcome with joy. He actually did it, he cast a real spell! His skill in magic increased from 20 to 21, not because he read a tome, but because he actually cast the damn spell. Though for Cedric, managing to read the tome was an achievement in itself.If he managed to create the spark, the fire will soon come.Without realizing it, our hero has applied one of the most important lessons in learning new skills: focused practice at the edge of your current ability.The game let him waste his savings on a spell tome, attempt to do something way beyond his skill and then fail in public. At the same time this pushed him to reconsider his options and start with a smaller step.Does this sound a bit familiar? I'm pretty sure we can all empathize with Cedric.Have you not bought a guitar thinking that you will become the next Jimmy Page? Have you not tried directly to play the most complicated solo you could think of and fail miserably? And only then, if you were actually persistent in your goal, you went back to square one and learned how to play a damn chord first?Come to think of it, there is not much difference between our fictional hero and ourselves.Each successful spell cast, every spark got him closer and closer to his goals. He continued to show up every dayuntil creating sparks became trivial.Cedric knew that casting the same spell over and over will eventually lead him to a plateau of his abilities so he continued to seek out harder and harder spells to master. He kept practicing and pushing himself and eventually he reached quite a respectable level in his magical abilities. His reading skill improved a lot as well.Did he become the most famous wizard in the land? Not quite. Getting better at anything takes persistence, but judging by his name, he has a great shot at making it.The same can be applied to us, the only difference is that we don’t have a skill bar that accurately tells us our level. We must continue to practice and show up without knowing exactly where we stand.Adding real life skill barsWhat we can accurately measure however is the time we take to practice in a focused, deliberate manner. I can’t build a skill bar that tells your competence, but I can build one that measures your dedication to leveling up.This is how the idea behind Levely was born. I realized that the reason for replaying the same RPGs over and over was because I felt the thrill of growing a character. Recently I decided that I’d rather that character be me.P.S. The mechanics of the game are even more in-depth than I’ve presented here. For example, tiredness has a huge effect on your success chances. Trying to cast a spell after sprinting up a hill will most likely fail.I also took a bit of literary freedom with the tome acquisition part. In Morrowind, spells are bought directly from vendors, though buying a spell still doesn’t guarantee you can cast it.

item.title: Prediction Market Odds Are Becoming News, but Their Context Is Getting Lost
item.author: EdwinMunyui
item.content:encoded: Prediction markets are building distribution faster than they are building standards for how their odds should be presented.A 70 per cent probability can look self-explanatory, but the number alone does not tell the audience the exact contract wording, when the price was captured, how much was traded, whether the move came from broad participation or a concentrated burst of buying, or who ultimately decides the outcome.The distinction becomes more important when market odds move into the media since the public-facing product is no longer the market alone. It includes the interface displaying the probability, the editorial decision to feature it and the distribution channel carrying it to a wider audience. Each hand-off can increase its reach while removing some of the context needed to interpret it.That tension surfaced recently after The that had stepped back from a broader partnership with Kalshi while remaining in discussions about advertising and other commercial opportunities. Staff had raised concerns about editorial independence, although the report’s source said those objections did not cause the decision.This week’s edition captures the broader issue: distribution is expanding, editorial boundaries are being tested and questions about market integrity are following the probability into public view.A Price Can Influence the Story About the PriceA gives this concern some useful scale. The researchers analysed 173.7 million signed Polymarket trades, 6,990 articles and 44,976 sharp price moves across 9,590 markets during 2024 and 2025.The paper classifies a sharp move, or “dislocation”, as a price change of at least five percentage points driven mainly by trading in one direction. It then compared the news coverage following each move with coverage during a similar period in the same market when no such movement occurred.Markets were about 33 per cent more likely to be cited after a dislocation. The timing also stood out, with seventy-four per cent of first citations appearing after the price had moved, while 58 per cent came more than a day later. Even after removing articles published on the same day as the move, the increase remained at 27 per cent.These results do not prove that the price movement caused the coverage or that anyone manipulated the market. The same news event could have prompted both the trading activity and the reporting. What the study does show is that a sharp, visible price move is often followed by a greater chance of that market being quoted by journalists.This creates the possibility of a feedback loop. A noticeable price movement gives journalists a reason to cover a market. That coverage brings the probability to a wider audience, which can attract more attention and trading activity. Future movements may then become even more likely to be treated as news.Prominent Markets Are More Likely to Get Picked UpAs markets became more prominent, it took far more trading activity to move their prices by five percentage points. The median rose from around $5,200 in the least prominent markets to $56,900 in the most prominent, an elevenfold increase.However, prominent markets were also more than twelve times as likely to be quoted in the news. The paper’s model found that a market’s existing prominence was a stronger predictor of media coverage than either the cost or size of the price movement.This creates an important distinction. Obscure markets may be cheaper to move, but few journalists notice them. Prominent markets are more expensive to move, yet any change in their odds has a much better chance of reaching a wider audience. Liquidity makes the signal more expensive to create, while media exposure makes that signal more valuable.The authors call this relationship “epistemic leverage.” Put simply, it compares the trading activity linked to a price movement with the likelihood that the resulting probability appears in news coverage.The point is that liquidity alone does not tell us how influential a market can become. We should also ask: once a probability leaves the platform, how widely will it be repeated and how much authority will people give it?The Missing Layer is Probability ProvenanceNewsrooms already have conventions for polls. Responsible coverage names the pollster, field dates, sample and margin of error. Prediction odds also need their own compact disclosure standard. The paper recommends attaching the venue, exact contract wording, timestamp, recent volume and an indication of extreme flow.Prediction Frontier would go slightly further by including visible depth and the named resolution source. Together, those details could form a more solid provenance trail for the number.The label should at least answer six fundamental questions:Where is the market, and can the reader inspect it?What exactly has to happen for “Yes” to resolve?When was the quoted price captured?What recent volume and available depth sit behind it?How large was the latest move?Was the flow concentrated, and who resolves the contract?This is not a case for keeping prediction markets out of journalism. Their prices can aggregate information quickly and expose changing expectations before slower indicators catch up.
