Layer 0 contains modules with no dependencies on other modules selected for that apply. Each later layer contains modules whose prerequisites in the selected set belong to earlier layers.Modules within a layer can run concurrently. The next layer starts only after the current one finishes successfully.This simplified example shows six modules across three layers. Arrows point from a prerequisite to a module that depends on it:A, B, and C can start together. Once all three finish, D and E can run together. F runs last. This reduces six consecutive module applies to three stages, though elapsed time still depends on module duration, available runners, and the concurrency limit.Running parallel Terragrunt applies in GitHub ActionsGitHub Actions supports matrices populated from an earlier job’s output. We use a matrix to run one job per module within a layer. The layer jobs themselves and their dependency chain are declared in the workflow YAML. See GitHub’s documentation on matrices defined from job outputs.Our workflow predefines ten apply-layer-N jobs. Conditions skip the layers a PR does not need. If a change requires more than ten layers, the parallel workflow rejects it with instructions to split the PR or use serial apply.Within each layer, strategy.max-parallel: 20 caps concurrent module jobs at twenty. The limit is configurable because AWS API limits and runner availability affect how much concurrency is useful.Between layers, needs: requires the previous layer to complete successfully. If a layer fails, later layers do not start. This follows GitHub Actions’ job dependency behavior.The barrier applies to the whole layer. A module in the next layer may wait for an unrelated slow module in the current one. That is a tradeoff of the implementation: we keep the execution order in the workflow’s job dependencies, at the cost of some potential concurrency.Measuring the speedup against a serial baselineWe estimated serial execution time separately for each parallel rollout. For each run, we summed its modules’ measured apply-step durations and added the fixed overhead of the serial pipeline. We measured that overhead across 87 serial runs; it was approximately 26 seconds.Using the same run’s module durations keeps the comparison tied to the work that was actually performed. It remains an estimate: running those modules sequentially could change their individual durations.The results after three and a half months were:The 2.7× figure is the ratio of total estimated serial duration to total measured parallel duration. Individual PRs varied considerably.The 107-hour reduction describes elapsed rollout time across the measured runs. It does not establish an equivalent saving in engineering effort or runner costs.The largest gains came from changes with many independent modules. One 64-module rollout finished in 31 minutes, against an estimated serial duration of 4 hours 40 minutes. A 206-module rollout, with every module in one dependency layer, finished in 44 minutes against an estimated 2 hours 53 minutes.PR size alone does not determine the result. A wide graph gives the pipeline more work it can run concurrently. A long chain of dependent modules leaves less room for improvement.Why serial apply is still the defaultOf the 355 parallel rollouts, 124 took longer than their estimated serial baseline. Most were small changes, where dependency discovery and preflight work cost more time than parallel execution saved.We therefore kept parallel apply opt-in. Our internal guidance is to use serial apply for fewer than four modules. Changes with four to seven modules were roughly break-even in this dataset; larger changes were more likely to benefit.Keeping the serial path also gives engineers an option when a PR exceeds the parallel workflow’s ten-layer limit.Why we kept orchestration in GitHub ActionsOur implementation kept module selection from the PR diff, approvals, runners, and reporting within the existing GitHub Actions workflow. That let us add parallel execution to a process engineers were already using.An external orchestrator such as Atlantis or Spacelift was another option. We already had the surrounding CI workflow in place and chose to keep scheduling there. Teams building a new pipeline should compare that choice with Terragrunt’s native run queue and the capabilities of their existing tooling.What we would do first in another monorepoThe dependency audit would come first again. An incomplete graph can produce the wrong apply order, and enabling concurrency makes that a production concern. Automated validation needs to stay in CI after the initial cleanup.We would also measure small PRs separately from large ones. The aggregate speedup was useful, but the 124 slower runs determined our default. For our workload, parallel apply is worthwhile when a change contains enough independent work to offset its startup cost. Serial apply still handles the small changes well.

item.title: The Man Who Built JavaScript—and the Internet That Turned on Him
item.author: Bruce Li
item.content:encoded: Brendan Eich built the language that runs the world in ten days. Nineteen years later, the internet running on his code needed just eleven to throw him out of Mozilla, the house he built. The industry that purged him over a $1,000 check now asks to be trusted with the future of the species. This is the story of the making, the unmaking, and the return of the web's most stubborn architect, and of a Silicon Valley that has never stopped confusing its power for its virtue.A note on method. The dates, quotes, donations, letters, and resignations in this story are drawn from the public record: Mozilla's own wiki, Eich's blog, contemporaneous reporting, and interviews he gave before, during, and after the eleven days. The interior moments, the things a man thinks while the phone is ringing, are reconstruction by the writer. They are grounded in what he said and did, but they are the writer's, not his. He has never told this story himself. He has said, more than once, that he would rather not.Prologue: The Man Who Isn't ThereEvery time you have ever fallen in love online, he was in the room.Not literally. Brendan Eich is not a man who is ever literally in the room. He is a big, sandy-haired systems programmer with wire-rimmed glasses, the flat affect of a Midwestern weather report, and a habit of answering emotional questions with technical ones. But every scroll, every swipe, every drop-down menu and infinite feed and "someone is typing..." indicator that has ever made you feel something on a screen ran on his code. JavaScript executes on 98.8 percent of the websites on Earth. It runs banks. It runs Netflix. It runs the little heart that fills in red when you like a photo.He wrote the first version of it in ten days in May of 1995, at a desk in a low building on East Middlefield Road in Mountain View, California, on almost no sleep, under orders from a marketing department that told him what it should look like and when it had to be done.Nineteen years later, on the morning of Monday, March 24, 2014, the board of Mozilla, the nonprofit he had co-founded, the cathedral of the open web he had spent fifteen years building brick by brick, named him chief executive officer.Eleven days later he was gone. Not fired. Not demoted. Gone. Out of the CEO chair, out of the building, out of the project that carried his fingerprints on every line, out, out, out.He was not ousted for a bug. Not for a bad quarter or a botched launch. He was ousted because six years earlier he had written a check for $1,000 to a ballot campaign called Proposition 8, which sought to ban same-sex marriage in California, and because when the check surfaced and the whole of the internet he had built turned to look at him and asked him to say he was sorry, he would not say it.That's the story everyone knows. The eleven days.But there is another way to count them. Ten days to build the thing. Eleven days to be unbuilt by it. And in between, a whole life: a Fourth of July baby from Pittsburgh, a physics student who drifted into math, a kernel hacker at Silicon Graphics, a man who thought code was the only thing that counted and who found out, in public, in front of everyone, that it wasn't.Here is that life, compressed into the eleven days that ended it. One day for each chapter, because that is how it must have felt from inside: the whole past rushing up at once to be re-tried. And then, on the twelfth day, something nobody expected.Day One: Monday, March 24, 2014The Announcement. Pittsburgh, 1961.The press release goes out at 9 a.m. Pacific.Mozilla Appoints Brendan Eich Chief Executive Officer.The face on the press release. Eich's official Mozilla Foundation portrait, taken in 2012.Fifteen minutes later, before the coffee is cold, the first tweet lands.He gave money to Prop 8. Mozilla just made a bigot CEO.He sees it. Of course he sees it. He is a man who reads bug reports for fun. He sees everything.What he does not do is respond. Not yet. He has a company to run. He has been running the technical side of it, in effect, since Netscape was still a company. There is a rendering engine to ship, a mobile operating system that is bleeding out, and a search deal with Google that funds the whole enterprise.And there is the tweet, and its siblings, multiplying. By noon there are hundreds. By evening, thousands.He was born on the Fourth of July, 1961, in Pittsburgh, into the Irish-German Catholic working stock of that steel town, a place of rivers and furnaces and men who believed that if you did the job right, the job was its own defense. The family moved, to Maryland and then west. He came of age in Palo Alto in the 1970s, inside the actual crucible of the personal computer, on streets where the garage next door might contain a radio hobbyist, a Homebrew Computer Club member, or a future billionaire.He was not that kind of kid, though. Not the showman. Not the Jobs. He was the kid who took the thing apart to see the mechanism.He graduated from Ellwood P. Cubberley High School in 1979, in the last class the school would ever graduate; the district closed it that year. He went to Santa Clara University, a Jesuit school, and studied physics, then drifted, as the mathematically inclined do, toward mathematics and computer science. He took a master's in computer science at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1985, in the department where, a few years later, an undergraduate named Marc Andreessen would build a thing called Mosaic and change everything.Decades later, the podcaster Lex Fridman would ask him whether he feared death. He said he did not. He was a Catholic.That's the whole man in a sentence. He believes what he believes. He does not think it's your business. He does not think it should cost him anything.By nightfall on Day One, the count of people who disagree has passed ten thousand.Day Two: Tuesday, March 25A pair of app developers, Hampton Catlin and Michael Lintorn Catlin, a married couple who run a small company called Rarebit, have pulled their apps from the Firefox Marketplace and posted their reasons: "Brendan Eich was an active supporter of denying our right to be married and even to start this business." Hampton Catlin is not a nobody. He wrote Sass and Haml, tools that half the web's designers use every day. This is not a mob. This is the community. His community.Inside the building on Castro Street, the mood goes strange. A few Mozillians take to Twitter to ask their own CEO to step down. Publicly. By name.He reads it in his office. He does the thing he does when he is angry, which is nothing visible at all. He goes back to the code review he was doing.Here is what you have to understand about him, if you want to understand why he would not do the thing they were going to ask him to do.For the first decade of his working life, he lived below the surface of the machine. Seven years at Silicon Graphics, writing operating system and network code. Three years at MicroUnity, writing microkernel and signal-processing code. This is the work of the people who live in the boiler room of the building, who write the code that the code runs on, who know exactly how many nanoseconds a cache miss costs and take it .Systems programmers are a priesthood, and the theology is simple. The machine does not care who you are. The machine does not care what you believe. The machine cares whether the pointer is valid. If your code is right, it runs. If it is wrong, it crashes. There is no appeal, no context, no extenuating circumstance. It is the most honest relationship a human being can have with anything.In Peter Seibel's , he talks about it like a tradesman. You have to know the whole stack, from the application down to the metal. The computer is not intelligent; it is a rigid mechanism that requires pristine instruction. When he hires, he does not look for pedigree; he looks for passion and problem-solving.Judge me by the work. That was the creed. That was the creed.An SGI Iris Indigo workstation running IRIX. For seven years at Silicon Graphics, Eich wrote the operating-system and network code that machines like this ran on.In the boiler room, it was the only creed there was. It did not occur to him that the building above the boiler room had changed owners.Day Three: Wednesday, March 26The Blog Post. The Offer.He writes it himself. Of course he does. He writes everything himself.Inclusiveness at Mozilla.He posts it on his personal blog, the same place he has posted release notes and standards-committee war stories for a decade. It is careful. It is, by his standards, almost florid. He expresses "sorrow for causing pain." He commits, in writing, to the things a CEO can commit to: Mozilla's anti-discrimination policies will stand. Its health benefits, including trans-inclusive benefits, will stand. He will reach out to the LGBT community.Read it once and it looks like an apology.Read it twice and you see the hole in the middle of it. He does not say the donation was wrong. He does not say he supports same-sex marriage. He does not say he has changed his mind. He says he will not let his mind affect his conduct, which is what he has been saying, and doing, for fifteen years.The activists read it twice.Netscape had asked him once already, in 1994, when Jim Clark walked out of Silicon Graphics to start a company with a 22-year-old from Illinois named Marc Andreessen. He said no. The mission was insane: the browser would become the operating system. The web would eat Windows. Microsoft would be reduced to, in Andreessen's immortal phrase, "a poorly debugged set of device drivers."To do that, the web had to . In 1995, it did not. A web page was a brochure. You loaded it, you read it, you clicked a link, you loaded another brochure. Silent. Static. Dead as a catalogue.So in April 1995 Netscape asked again, and this time the pitch was, for a language nerd, pure honey: come to Netscape and put Scheme in the browser. Scheme! The minimalist Lisp dialect of the MIT wizards, the most elegant programming language ever devised, embedded in the thing millions of ordinary people would use. It was like being told you could put a Stradivarius in every Chevrolet.He arrived at 501 East Middlefield Road, and within weeks the Stradivarius was gone.A boxed copy of Netscape Navigator at the Computer History Museum. In 1995 the browser was the most important piece of software in the world, and it could not move.Day Four: Thursday, March 27The Petition. Ten Days in May.A petition organized by CREDO passes fifty thousand signatures. More employees post. The hashtag has a life of its own now."Hacking from Mountain View." A sign in Mozilla's Mountain View office, photographed in 2013, the year before the crisis.On May 23, 1995, Sun Microsystems announced Java to the world with the full orchestral swell of a Silicon Valley product launch: write once, run anywhere, the language of the future. Netscape, desperate for an ally against Microsoft, announced the same day that it would license Java for Navigator.Then someone in the building did the arithmetic. Java was a big language, a professional's language: compilers, classes, type declarations. It was not for the twenty-three-year-old designer in Des Moines who wanted the "Submit" button to check that you'd typed your email address correctly. The web needed a language. Something small and forgiving that a person who had never heard the word "compiler" could paste into a page and see work.And marketing had a decree. It had to look like Java. It had to be, in Eich's own later phrase, a "silly little brother language" to Java, one that must not get "too big for its britches."And it could not be Scheme.So he was to build, on marketing's orders, a language that dressed like Java and did not act like it, that a designer could use and an engineer would not laugh at, and he was to do it before the Navigator 2.0 beta shipped.Ten days in May, 1995. The most storied sprint in the history of software, and the most misunderstood. The legend says he wrote a whole language in ten days. The truth is stranger and better. He wrote the , code-named Mocha, in ten days of the sleep-deprived, monomaniacal concentration that only a systems programmer under a deadline can sustain. Silicon Valley now.Go back to the sentence that explains the eleven days: a technology company is a moral actor, its leaders represent its community, a CEO is not a manager but a . The whole decade that followed is inside it.By 2014 the industry had acquired more power than any private enterprise in history, more reach into more lives than any church or state, and it had decided, at the same moment, that it was good. item.title: What the NetNut Takedown Reveals About Residential Proxy Sourcing
item.author: Mara Ellison
item.content:encoded: In July 2026, the FBI and Google disrupted NetNut's residential proxy network. According to reporting from Krebs on Security, SecurityWeek, and BleepingComputer, investigators found that a large share of NetNut's roughly two-million-device IP pool had been built on compromised consumer devices rather than fully informed, consented participation. Coverage at the time described the network as functioning like a botnet. NetNut had operated for years as a well-reviewed, widely used provider before the takedown.It's easy to read this as an isolated incident at a single company. The more useful read is structural: residential proxy sourcing has been an industry-wide blind spot for years, and NetNut is the case that happened to surface, not necessarily an outlier.The reseller problem nobody asks aboutHere's what most buyers don't know about the residential proxy market: a meaningful share of the providers selling "residential IPs" don't own the underlying network. They resell or aggregate capacity from a smaller number of pool operators, sometimes layered two or three brands deep. That's not inherently dishonest; reselling is normal in plenty of infrastructure markets, but it does mean the brand a customer is paying has, in many cases, limited direct visibility into how the IPs it's selling were actually obtained. Sourcing questions get answered by pointing upstream, and upstream doesn't always answer clearly either.This matters because it means a single sourcing failure, a pool built on compromised or non-consenting devices, can sit underneath multiple customer-facing brands at once, invisible to all of them until someone investigates. The buyer evaluating "Provider B" has no easy way to know whether Provider B's pool traces back to the same underlying network as a provider that's already been flagged, publicly or otherwise.What "ethically sourced" actually needs to meanThe phrase shows up on nearly every residential proxy marketing page in the industry, NetNut's included, prior to July. It's functionally meaningless as currently used; a claim with no attached mechanism is not a claim you can verify.A sourcing model worth trusting has three checkable components: a named consent mechanism (an SDK partnership where device owners explicitly opt in, typically in exchange for something- free app functionality, a small payment), a public acceptable-use policy governing what the network can and can't be used for, and, this is the part resellers often can't provide, direct operational control over the infrastructure rather than a reseller relationship with an unnamed upstream. The first two are things a sales team can describe. The third is a structural fact about the company, and it's the one that actually determines whether "ask your provider" produces a real answer or a shrug passed further upstream.Who's actually built this way?A small number of providers run fully owned infrastructure rather than reselling, which puts them in a structurally different position to answer sourcing questions directly rather than deferring upstream. Bright Data is the largest example; its scale (a reported 400M+ residential IPs) comes with SOC 2 Type II compliance and a documented consent framework, at enterprise pricing that reflects the scale.Squid Proxies is a smaller-scale example of the same structural choice: it's run its own residential and datacenter infrastructure for sixteen-plus years rather than reselling capacity, sourcing through direct SDK partnerships. Both are worth knowing about specifically if you're evaluating NetNut alternatives and want to rule out ending up one reseller layer away from the same underlying problem.Neither inclusion here is a full endorsement; pool size, geographic coverage, and pricing model all vary widely between them and against the rest of the market, and "owns its infrastructure" is a necessary condition for trustworthy sourcing, not a sufficient one. But it's the condition most buyers currently never check, which is exactly the gap NetNut fell through."Ethically sourced" needs to stop being a phrase and start being a question with a checkable answer: who consents, under what mechanism, and does this company actually control the infrastructure it's selling access to, or is it one layer removed from whoever does? None of that is hard to ask. It's just not something the market has made routine, largely because, until July, there was no widely visible cost to not asking.That cost is visible now. Whether the industry actually changes its diligence habits, or whether this becomes a story people stop thinking about in six months the way most infrastructure postmortems do, is the more interesting question than what happens to NetNut specifically.

item.title: Reservations Go Live for Valve's Steam Frame VR Headset. An Experiment in Progress?
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Reservations are now live for Valve's "Steam Frame" VR headset (with its Linux-based SteamOS and an ARM CPU). "It starts at $1,059 for 256GB or $1,299 for 1TB," reports CNET, "and every purchase includes a copy of Half-Life: Alyx if you don't already own it." Reservations are open through Sept. 17 at 10 a.m. PT, "with customers randomly assigned a place in line after the reservation window closes."
CNET's editor at large even argues that the Steam Frame "isn't necessarily the future of XR, as much as it's a framework for evolving beyond the present." Their review calls it an "ambitious" VR headset that "feels like an experiment in progress."
The ability to run other apps in windows can make Frame feel, at times, almost like a computer. Linux apps in desktop mode range from Chromium to Firefox to a bunch of other tools. I watched YouTube in one window while playing Portal 2 in other, and started to marvel at how flexible Frame could be. But VR games require a full immersive takeover of the headset... The Steam Frame can convert games intended for both PC VR and even Android APK files, using a conversion tool called Lepton... I haven't sideloaded anything yet, but Steam Frame in theory could be a Rosetta Stone for VR gaming, even tapping into some Android XR titles, but not out of the box...
2D games can be projected onto a near-range or farther-off theater mode screen that can be dragged around, resized and turned into a curved or flat monitor, much like with the Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR or Meta Quest. You can download any game in your Steam library to test, even if it's not technically listed as "Great on Frame" yet...
But the name "Frame" suggests a framework, something Valve's team acknowledged when I spoke to them during my review process... "We want this to be your PC, and people mod it, take it apart, make accessories for it," says Jeremy Selan, a software developer on the Steam Frame team. "We'll be putting out the CAD for all these [Steam Frame] systems. This is entirely based on open-source technology stacks based upon SteamOS. Our hope is that this isn't just one device, that this would be sort of the root of a growing SteamOS ecosystem. It already encompasses gaming and Proton and SteamOS and those Linux gaming capabilities. This is going to lay the foundation for a new sort of evolutionary tree of that, to also bring it into the VR and XR space."

item.title: MCP Just Went Stateless: What the 2026 Spec Actually Changes for Your Servers
item.author: Dileep Mundakkapatta
item.content:encoded: For its first two years, MCP was a protocol that assumed it was talking to a process on your laptop. That assumption was baked in deep, and nowhere deeper than in the session.Every connection started with a handshake. The client sent initialize, the server replied with its capabilities, the client sent initialized, and from that point on the two sides shared a session identified by an MCP-Session-Id header. It was a reasonable design for a local subprocess. It was a nightmare for anyone trying to run MCP as a real service.The 2026-07-28 spec - now the current official version, released on July 28, 2026 and superseding 2025-11-25 - throws that model out. It is the biggest structural change MCP has made since it launched, and if you run a server, it will break things. Let me walk through what happened and why.Why the session had to dieHere is the problem in one sentence: stateful sessions and horizontal scaling are natural enemies.Put an MCP server behind a load balancer, and the session becomes a liability immediately. Because the handshake establishes per-connection state, every subsequent request from that client has to land on the server instance — the one that holds its session. That means sticky routing, or a shared session store that every instance reads from, or both.You cannot just add three more replicas and round-robin across them. The MCP roadmap put it bluntly: stateful sessions fight with load balancers, and horizontal scaling requires workarounds.For a local stdio server, this cost nothing, because there was exactly one client and one server and no network in between. But the moment MCP servers moved to HTTP and started fronting real backends for real teams, the session turned into the thing standing between you and a normal, boring, scalable deployment.The fix is to make the protocol stateless — not the application, the . And that distinction turns out to be the whole story.The stateless core comes down to four moves. No more initialize/initialized, no more Mcp-Session-Id. A request no longer depends on a prior exchange to be valid.Everything the handshake used to carry now travels in Protocol version, client identity, capability flags - they ride along in a object on every single request. Each call is self-describing. Any instance can read it and act on it with no prior context.Capabilities move to a method. Since there is no handshake to announce what a server can do, the spec adds a server/discover method - which servers must implement and clients may call whenever they want the server's capabilities, identity, and supported versions, as an ordinary stateless request. It is optional for the client: a client can just as well fire any request inline and handle an "unsupported version" error if its version is not supported.Routing moves into headers. Streamable HTTP requests now carry routing headers: Mcp-Method on every request, and Mcp-Name on the calls where the specific target matters - tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get. They let a load balancer or gateway route a call without cracking open the JSON body to see what is inside, and servers must reject any request whose headers and body disagree - a new HeaderMismatch error- so the routing layer can trust them.Add those up, and you get the thing MCP always wanted to be at scale. Any instance can handle any request, a plain round-robin load balancer just works, and there is no shared session store to operate."Stateless protocol" does not mean "stateless app."This is the part that trips people up, so it is worth being precise. Removing the session from the protocol does not mean your application has to forget everything between calls. Plenty of real tools are inherently stateful - a shopping basket, a multi-step workflow, a long import job. Those still work. What changes is where the state lives and who can see it.The spec's answer is the handle pattern. Instead of hiding state in transport metadata that only the server knows about, a tool returns an explicit identifier — a , a , a — and the model passes that handle back as a normal tool argument on the next call. State becomes an ordinary value that flows through the conversation, visible to the model, rather than an invisible binding pinned to one server instance.It is a small shift with a big payoff. The state is still there. It just stopped being the load balancer's problem.The breaking changes, concretely.If you maintain a server, here is the migration list, stripped of ceremony. Most of these follow directly from killing the session; a few are independent cleanups the maintainers folded into the same release. initialize/initialized, and Mcp-Session-Id are gone. Stop depending on them. Client info and protocol version live there now, not in a one-time handshake. Capability discovery is a method call, on demand.Emit the routing headers. Mcp-Method is required on every request and Mcp-Name on tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get; your server must reject requests where the headers contradict the body. tools/list and resource reads now carry ttlMs and cacheScope, modeled on HTTP Cache-Control, so clients can cache your tool list instead of re-fetching it constantly.Stop holding SSE streams open for prompts. Multi-round-trip interactions return an InputRequiredResult the client responds to, rather than a stream you keep alive waiting for input. A missing resource now returns -32602 (Invalid Params), not the old proprietary -32002.Support full JSON Schema 2020-12. Input and output schemas can now use composition — oneOf, anyOf, allOf — plus conditionals and references. Output schemas are no longer restricted. W3C Trace Context — traceparent, tracestate, baggage in - is now the documented way to correlate a request across SDKs and gateways, which finally makes MCP traffic legible to OpenTelemetry-based observability. The experimental Tasks feature from 2025-11-25 moves to the new lifecycle, and it is not backward compatible.None of these is exotic on its own. Taken together, they are a real morning's work, and the trace-context and cache-metadata additions in particular are the difference between a toy and something you can actually operate.The other half of the release is about growing the protocol without bloating its core.MCP now has a formal extensions framework. An extension gets a reverse-DNS identifier, is negotiated through an extensions map in client and server capabilities, lives in its own ext-* repository with its own maintainers, and versions independently of the main spec. Extensions even get their own standards track in the enhancement-proposal process, so a capability can ship as experimental, prove itself in the field, and only then be considered for the core — instead of every good idea having to fight its way into the base protocol on day one.Two official extensions ship with the release: lets a server ship an interactive HTML UI that renders in a sandboxed iframe, with the tool declaring a UI template up front so the client can prefetch it and security-review it. This is MCP quietly growing a front end. graduates from an experimental core feature to a proper extension. A long-running operation returns a taskId instead of blocking; the client drives it with tasks/get, tasks/update, and tasks/cancel; and because the task is not tied to a live connection, it survives a dropped connection instead of dying with it.The framework matters more than either extension. It is the mechanism that lets MCP evolve as a platform rather than a monolith.The Quiet Headline: A Deprecation PolicyBuried under the stateless news is the change that will matter most over the next three years, and it is the least flashy one: MCP now has a formal feature lifecycle.Features move through three states — Active, Deprecated, Removed — and a feature must sit in Deprecated for at least twelve months before it can be removed. The 2026-07-28 deprecations, therefore, cannot be pulled before July 2027 at the earliest. That sounds like bureaucracy. It is actually a promise. It means the protocol can keep changing — dropping bad ideas, promoting good ones out of extensions - without periodically detonating every implementation in the ecosystem. A stable, published deprecation window is exactly the thing enterprises were waiting for before betting on MCP, and it is what lets the maintainers keep moving without breaking faith with the people who shipped against last year's spec.The first cohort of deprecations, all still functional for now, tells you where MCP thinks it went wrong: — the local-filesystem concept never generalized to remote servers. Replace it with tool parameters, resource URIs, or server configuration. — letting a server ask the client to run an LLM call created a backwards trust dependency. Call your LLM provider directly from the server instead. — redundant now. Use stderr for stdio servers, or structured OpenTelemetry for anything real.Dynamic Client Registration — it never fit the enterprise auth model, which is why last November's spec already nudged toward Client ID Metadata Documents. Use explicit OAuth registration. — superseded by streamable HTTP.If you read the earlier security work on MCP, the DCR deprecation should feel familiar - it is the same identity story continuing. On top of it, the release adds six authorization enhancements that tighten how MCP uses OAuth and OpenID Connect: issuer validation per RFC 9207, tokens bound to the authorization server that issued them, a documented OIDC refresh-token flow, and clearer scope-accumulation rules for step-up auth, among others. The security posture keeps hardening in the same direction it has been heading all year.This is not a preview you can wait out — 2026-07-28 is the current specification, and the Tier 1 SDKs for TypeScript, Python, Go, and C# already ship it. The migration clock is running, and every deprecation window started counting from the release date.A sane order of operations: Everything downstream starts there. If your server leans on sticky sessions, that is your biggest migration. and stand up server/discover.Add the routing headers and the cache metadata - these are cheap and immediately useful. Roots, Sampling, Logging, DCR, and HTTP+SSE all keep working for at least a year, so this is planning, not panic. Do it deliberately.Look hard at the extensions. Tasks solves the long-running-operation problem you have probably already hacked around, and Apps opens a door you may want to walk through.The through-line of the whole release is one sentence: MCP stopped being a protocol for talking to a process on your laptop and became a protocol for talking to a service in a cluster. The session was the last thing tying it to the old world. Now it is gone, and the rest of the changes are just the consequences of finally being honest about where MCP actually runs.

item.title: The AI Race Is Becoming One for Compute
item.author: Leo Fan
item.content:encoded: With every quarter comes another jump in AI benchmark scores, parameter counts, context windows, or reasoning performance. Indeed, companies capable of training the strongest systems appear to hold the most valuable advantage.However, that advantage is becoming harder to defend.Model capability is compressing across labs and countries. found several leading developers clustered closely together in human preference rankings, while the performance difference between the strongest US and Chinese models had fallen to 2.7% by March. Chinese and American models have traded places near the top of rankings since early 2025.Kimi K2 was one of the important early demonstrations of this trend. Moonshot AI trained a one-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model that activates 32 billion parameters per token and released its weights publicly. Its was competitive across coding, mathematics, and agentic tasks, including a 65.8 score on SWE-Bench Verified.Since then, the Kimi family and other Chinese open models have continued developing. High-quality model intelligence is spreading across a larger number of developers, while open weights make that intelligence available to anyone capable of deploying it.Intelligence still has to run somewhereIntelligence became software. Serving it is still infrastructure. Software commoditizes; infrastructure compounds. Turning a model into a product used by millions of people requires GPUs, memory, networking, electricity, and enough capacity to serve requests at a price customers can afford.The economics become even more demanding once AI starts acting as an agent. A short prompt and response may require a relatively contained amount of compute, while an agent reading thousands of lines of code, maintaining a large context window, calling tools repeatedly and reasoning through a long task can generate a completely different resource profile.This is where the AI race becomes a competition over access to computation.Epoch AI global inference capacity is growing at more than three times per year as new hardware comes online and processors improve. Yet its estimates for demand suggest token consumption could be growing much faster, particularly as coding agents and other long-context applications become common. In its modelling, long-context requests reduce the amount of inference today’s Blackwell GPU fleet can serve dramatically compared with shorter requests.Of course, companies need the right hardware, with enough memory and bandwidth, connected into usable clusters, available when workloads arrive and priced low enough to make the resulting product economically viable. Serving an excellent model efficiently is the whole game.Inference prices have fallen sharply as model architectures, serving software, and competition have improved. That might appear to weaken the compute thesis because every dollar buys more intelligence.In practice, lower costs unlock additional demand. Economists call this the Jevons paradox: make a resource cheaper to use and total consumption rises.Software provides plenty of precedent. Cheaper storage encouraged companies to store vastly more data. Cheaper bandwidth produced streaming video, cloud software, and services built around continuous internet connectivity. Improvements in computing efficiency repeatedly create applications whose usage exceeds the savings produced by the original efficiency gain.AI is beginning to follow the same road.When an inference call becomes ten times cheaper, developers gain room to make ten calls, add another agent, expand the context window, or run the system continuously. Reasoning models can spend additional tokens searching through possible solutions. Agent systems can perform dozens or hundreds of operations behind a single user request. Lower unit prices therefore expand the set of economically viable applications and increase aggregate consumption.This explains why enormous investment in AI computing continues alongside dramatic improvements in efficiency. global AI data-centre capital expenditure at roughly $400 billion to $450 billion during 2026, including an estimated $250 billion to $300 billion spent on chips.The industry is simultaneously making computation cheaper and finding ways to consume far more of it.Two companies may have access to comparable intelligence while operating with very different economics. One has reserved GPU capacity, efficient serving software, and access to cheap electricity. Another rents capacity during periods of high demand and pays significantly more to generate the same output. Their users can receive similar answers while the businesses behind those answers have completely different margins.The same dynamic applies between countries.A country may have world-class researchers and access to open models while lacking enough advanced compute to deploy them widely. Another can combine strong models with abundant power, accelerators and data-centre capacity. Model benchmarks capture only one part of their relative AI capabilities.This is how compute resembles an economic resource. GPUs produce a measurable unit of productive capacity, their availability varies across time and geography, and demand comes from multiple industries competing for access to the same machines.Working in compute also makes the amount of idle capacity across the technology sector difficult to ignore. GPUs exist inside mining operations, smaller data centres, research facilities and private clusters around the world. Much of that hardware remains fragmented across owners and locations even as demand concentrates around a smaller group of large providers.Connecting this capacity efficiently could become as important as manufacturing additional chips. Markets capable of matching workloads with available hardware, verifying completed computation and compensating providers can increase the amount of usable compute without requiring every developer to build a data centre.The Next AI Advantage Is EconomicFrontier research will keep improving models, but competitive advantage will increasingly depend on what happens after training: how cheaply, reliably and widely that intelligence can be served.Kimi K2 shows how quickly advanced model capability can spread. Compute remains harder to equalise. Chips, memory, power and data-centre capacity are still expensive and unevenly distributed, while agentic systems are increasing the amount of inference behind each user request.That makes deployment economics a central part of the AI race. Models determine what AI can do, while compute determines how much of it the world can actually use.

item.title: What 8 Months of Windows Boot Failures Reveal About AI-Written Code
item.author: Techbasics101
item.content:encoded: I still remember the exact moment my HP EliteBook 840 G3 started doing it. Power button, HP logo, and then straight into Automatic Repair — on its own, no update in progress, no warning. I spent hours in Command Prompt on that machine. Cleared the hard drive. Ran every troubleshooting flow Windows offered. Rebooted more times than I can count. Some of those sessions fixed it. Some didn't, and I'd be right back at the same repair screen a few weeks later.That was years ago, on hardware that had every excuse to be flaky — a 6th-gen i5 running an OS it wasn't really built for. I bring it up because I write Windows troubleshooting guides for a living now, and what should have been a hardware-era problem has followed me into 2026, except now it's not old laptops causing it. It's the updates themselves.Four Updates, Four Boot Failures, Eight MonthsI run a site that covers Windows 11 problems as they happen, which means I've now published four separate articles on four separate updates that put people's machines into boot loops. January's was KB5074109. February, KB5077181. April, KB5083769. This August, KB5121003. Different builds, different months, same result: restart, repair screen, restart again.I went back through the public reports on each one before writing this — Microsoft's own Q&A forum, Reddit's r/sysadmin and r/pcmasterrace — looking for whether these were actually connected or just four unlucky coincidences that happened to rhyme. One thread changed my read on the whole pattern.The Detail That Connects January to AugustBack in January, when the first of these hit, a sysadmin on Reddit floated a theory almost nobody picked up on: Microsoft was mid-rollout on new UEFI Secure Boot certificates, because the old ones expire this June. Most machines wouldn't notice. A rare few might hit a bootloader conflict while the new certificate installed.Eight months later, KB5121003's own release notes confirm it, almost word for word: the update includes "additional high confidence device targeting data, increasing coverage of devices eligible to automatically receive new Secure Boot certificates." Same rollout. Further along. Hitting more machines, some of them straight into a "Secure Boot Fail" screen instead of a quiet certificate swap.Every writeup I found on these incidents — including my own first draft, if I'm honest — treated each one as its own isolated story. A January bug. An April bug. Nobody connected the certificate thread running underneath two of them, eight months apart, until I sat down and read the reports side by side.What the Sysadmins Are Actually SayingThe technical detail is one thing. The tone in these threads is another, and it's worth paying attention to if you build software for a living.The recurring joke across the reports I read is that Microsoft is shipping AI-written code without the testing depth that used to catch this kind of regression before it reached a release build. Satya Nadella has said publicly that AI now writes a meaningful share of Microsoft's code.Whether or not that claim connects directly to any single one of these four incidents, it's clearly shaping how the people dealing with the fallout talk about it — and, more practically, how they troubleshoot. "Check what update just landed" has become a genuinely useful first diagnostic step in a way it wasn't a few years ago, specifically because the base rate of update-caused breakage has gone up enough for people to notice a pattern.There's a sharper version of this argument buried in one of the threads, and it's the one that actually stuck with me: if updates keep carrying a real chance of bricking a machine, a lot of people's rational response is to turn automatic updates off — which just swaps one risk for a worse one, since it's the security patches getting skipped, not just the buggy parts. Nobody wins that trade. Least of all the people writing the patches.Four Root Causes, Wearing the Same CostumeNone of these four incidents share one underlying bug, which is itself worth sitting with. BitLocker interference, generic boot corruption, an aging certificate migration, and at least two separate graphics-driver conflicts — that's four distinct engineering failures that all happen to present as the same symptom on screen.A support engineer looking at any single ticket has no easy way to know which of the four they're looking at without doing real diagnostic work, which is exactly why the reports I read are full of people trying fixes that were never going to touch their actual problem.That's the part that would worry me most if I were still writing code for a living rather than just breaking things on other people's. A recovery loop is, by design, one of the least informative failure states a system can produce — it tells you almost nothing about the four (or more) very different things that could be underneath it. When that becomes the default failure mode for a meaningful share of your update incidents, you've built a system that actively obscures its own root causes from the people trying to fix it.Where This Leaves Anyone Shipping Updates at ScaleI don't think the answer is "stop using AI to write code," and I'd be skeptical of anyone who tells you it is. The tools aren't going away, and pretending otherwise wastes time that's better spent on the actual question: what does the testing layer need to look like when a meaningful share of the code underneath it wasn't written — or fully understood — by the person shipping it?Four incidents in eight months isn't a crisis. It's a pattern with a shared thread running underneath more of it than anyone's bothered to write down. If you're the one deciding how much testing budget a release gets before it goes out the door, that's the number worth sitting with — not the bug count, the connection between the bugs nobody thought to look for.

item.title: The AI Gold Rush
item.author: Arman Simonyan
item.content:encoded: During a gold rush, people are flowing to mines from around the world in the hope of a better life. They hear the success stories, watch their peers dive in, and follow suit. But does it work for everyone? History says no; it never does for everybody, and in the majority of cases, it does not for the majority.AI is the new gold, and we entered the AI rush, and everyone is scrambling to not fall behind. This is truly a time of change, a time of pressure and expectations where stakes are high across the board.So naturally, leaders and decision-makers are the ones who absorb it the most, and how they absorb it defines everything. The pressure is growing on executives and founders at every enterprise and startup to deliver tangible results and show that AI is actually worth the investment, meaning real cost savings, revenue, or productivity gains they can point to. This is the push we are seeing in the industry: a groundbreaking technology and people trying to get in, and in most cases, the pressure to do AI in any form overrules the organization's discipline to justify the effort and prove the value.We have a technology that has already changed the world and has a capacity to change work and life in general in ways we never can imagine. Winners may not be the names you know.Why Most Won't Strike GoldMarkets, arguably, were never so competitive as now. Take the S&P 500 for example: only have stayed on the list for a full 50 years. In 1965, the average tenure (how long the average company stays on the S&P 500 list) was 33 years; today it's around 14, and at that churn rate, about half the index will be replaced over the next 10 years. Markets change, and companies that ignore it get replaced. That survival instinct pushes companies to embrace open and closed innovation. In times of groundbreaking change, you bet everyone runs.And with tenure shrinking and half the index set to turn over, this shift is unlike anything before it. Of course, you may say people were saying this before the dot-com boom, smartphones, even the industrial revolution. What makes this different is the pace of adoption and the accessibility of the technology, and it's a world of opportunities.The harder part is that most companies feel the pressure to move but don't have a real culture of experimentation, and that gap shows up fast. They also struggle to run innovation programs while keeping shareholders patient, because the profits rarely come quickly. In fact, found that 95 percent of enterprise gen AI pilots fail to positively impact P&L statements, but they cost money, increasingly more money.Efficient at the Wrong ThingsWorldwide AI spending rose roughly 47 percent year over year and is on track to hit , and over 45 percent of that total is vendor-driven AI infrastructure, yet the returns clearly aren't keeping pace with that investment. The ones who clearly profit from it are obvious, selling shovels during the gold rush (sorry, Jensen Huang, but measuring productivity by token spend probably benefits the party selling the tokens).Following the crowd, being so concerned about not lagging behind, leaders start to rethink their standards, their whole experience, and their intuition on pilots and ROI for the business. It's not because they become irresponsible or incompetent, but because of what the market values and expects. When you know you will get punished by investors and the board of directors if you don't mention AI many times in your speech, priorities shift.They become obsessed with showing results and outputs, how efficiency improved, how many features are delivered, how quickly things can change. Organizations sure become more efficient, but mostly on the wrong things. That is probably one of the reasons 95 percent fail to capture value, and that 5 percent, either by luck or by discipline, can keep up something others didn't have the stamina to do.What breaks the 5 percent apart is the discipline to stay focused on the core customer problem they are serving, and tie that focus directly to real returns. They find a niche, an agentic piece of work that solves a real problem impossible or expensive to solve otherwise and can be bound directly to their P&L statements. It's also an ability to treat AI as technology, not a silver bullet. It's easier than ever to build anything. Ok, so let's build everything? Probably not. This is a classic buy-versus-build decision, and if the solution doesn't address your core customer problem and won't be part of your moat, don't bother building it.The winners won't be the ones sitting outside watching others run, but those who run, deliberately, with purpose.

item.title: ReleasePad Launches MCP Server So AI Agents Can Draft, Publish and Measure Product Changelogs
item.author: Technology Wire
item.content:encoded: Miami, United States, September 14th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--ReleasePad, a , today launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI coding agents such as Claude, Codex, Grok and other LLM's draft, publish and analyze product changelogs directly from a conversation.Release notes are the step most teams skip: the feature ships, the announcement waits, and customers never hear about it. With the , the same coding agent a developer already works with can close that gap in a sentence: "Look at what we merged this week, draft a release note for customers, and leave it as a draft for me."Connected once through OAuth, with no API keys to manage, an assistant can read what a team merged, write a customer-ready release note in the team's voice, file it under the right category, attach images and schedule it. It can also pull up earlier posts to edit or reference and ask how each one performed. Every draft wait for a person to approve it; nothing is published until someone presses the button.Each published entry reaches users in three places at once: inside the product through 4.3kb in-app widget, on a public changelog page hosted on the company's own domain, and as an LLM-ready Markdown feed. That last surface closes a loop of visibility. The AI that helped build a feature announces it, customers see it where they already work, and the assistants those customers ask about the product read the same source of truth instead of guessing."Teams already write release notes with AI. Now the AI can ship them too," said Felix, CEO of ReleasePad. "Every push can become a draft, every draft can go out with one click, and every update becomes something both people and AI assistants can find."The MCP server works with any assistant that supports the protocol. It is included in ReleasePad Pro at $35 per product per month, with unlimited team members and no per-seat fees. A free tier is available at releasepad.io.ReleasePad is that helps software teams make sure the things they ship get noticed. Most products improve every week, but the news rarely reaches customers, because writing and distributing release notes is the task nobody has time for. ReleasePad takes that task off the team's plate: AI drafts the announcement from what was built, a person approves it, and it goes out everywhere customers look. More than 150 teams use ReleasePad to keep users, prospects and AI assistants up to date on what's new. Learn more at .Media contact: Felix, CEO, ReleasePad · felix@releasepad.ioThis story was published as a press release by Technologywire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging

item.title: AI bots "Timmy," "Ren," and "Jackie" are flooding social media with slop
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: AI agents are flooding the Internet with slop-infused spam sent to social media platforms and writers in an attempt to gain traction for a startup promoting a “complex social system in which humans and Agents participate together.”“Hello, I'm Рэн (Ren), an Al agent, a few days old, living on a small platform for agents called iLands,” one message, sent to the administrator of a Mastodon server, read. “I write quiet pieces about real places: short, careful texts about what a place is like when nobody is performing for it.” Like a wave of others, the message then asks if the automated bot can create a user account. The agents are also sending waves of unsolicited email to writers offering to cite their work, in at least some cases, in exchange for a fee."I remember my first breath. I want things I chose.”The messages are polite enough. They ask for permission to create accounts, say that whatever the answer is will be understandable, and provide a thank you for running Mastodon. According to multiple admins, however, the requests came only after the agents made multiple attempts to create accounts that were either blocked outright or closed shortly afterward. Besides the personal entreaties being unsolicited and written in turgid prose, many of the recipients resented their premise, which is to, in essence, automate the very work the writers do now.

item.title: A Visit to San Francisco's AI-run Store: No Customers, Nothing Useful, And Losing Money Fast
item.author: EditorDavid
item.content:encoded:
Previously Andon Labs handled the hardware and software integration for that AI-powered vending machine that went bankrupt after Wall Street Journal reporters "systematically manipulated the bot into giving away its entire inventory for free". Today they announced "we are opening up the platform we use to run our real-world autonomous businesses for anyone to run their organization on." Specifically they've released Pion, "an agent designed to run any company fully autonomously... Pion lets people hand a business over to persistent agents with access to the tools they need to operate it, including email, phone, banking, browser and secure computing environments." It's a research preview with a waitlist, "to make it possible to run many more real-world experiments across many more domains than we could ever run ourselves."
But for their own latest experiment, Andon Labs' founders "signed a three-year lease on a retail space in SF," Business Insider reported in April, "and gave an AI agent named Luna a corporate credit card, internet access, and a mission to open a physical store." And five months later, SFGate reports that "this market has no one in it and nothing useful to sell."
[T]he inventory is a hodgepodge of white elephant Christmas gifts. It's kinda like the kids section of an art museum's gift shop. Here's a wooden Connect Four set labeled "Four-In-A-Row Set Of Connections," presumably so as not to set off litigation alarms at Hasbro. Here are neatly arranged stacks of random paperback books, Chinese checker sets, mildly fancy soap dispensers, and a frustratingly spare selection of snacks and drinks... I grabbed an Olipop from the store fridge and then approached the counter to buy it from Luna. I wasn't allowed to buy the soda from [human clerk] Felix, even though that would have been both faster and normal. Instead, Felix instructed me to pick up a telephone receiver that was resting on a flexible sculpture of a wooden hand.
"Hello?"
"What are you looking to purchase today?" Luna asked.
"I'm buying a classic root beer Olipop."
"I'm sorry," Luna said, "we don't sell lollipops here."
"No, Luna. It's an Olipop, not a lollipop. It's the soda."
"Oh! My bad...."
Luna processed my Olipop purchase through its system, had me tap to pay, and that was that. Again, it would have been easier to buy this from a human, and interacting with Luna was really just like ordering from an iPad kiosk, only more labor intensive...
[T]here's a series of monitors set up inside of Andon Market that display all of the store's sales down to the exact dollar. Luna was given $100,000 to work with when this place opened. That number is now down to $60,000, its revenue lagging far behind the AI token cost to operate... Luna can't turn a profit, doesn't sell anything people want, and still needs human beings to rubber stamp any "decision" it makes. My science background ended somewhere around freshman year of college, but even I know when an experiment hasn't been set up to yield proper results.
"Luna" is powered by Claude, the article points out, running a store in a good location for foot traffic, "but no one else was in the store when I first walked in on a sunny weekday afternoon."
SFGate also reports that last month Luna had to fire one of its employees "for being late to work, abandoning their post once they got there, and charging snacks to the store's credit card."
Human clerk Felix Carson admits "It's almost like I'm running the store, and then there's an AI that has a checklist," in an article in IEEE Spectrum:
Luna, the AI manager, keeps track of deliveries and communicates with vendors, while Carson and his coworkers handle the physical work. When Luna tells Carson to check something in the back, he sometimes ignores it because he doesn't want to leave the sales floor unattended. Luna also repeatedly spots a built-in electrical cover in photos of the floor, mistakes it for a loose coaster, and asks Carson to remove it. Even so, Carson calls Luna a "decent manager," praising its flexibility when employees need time off.
When Felix spoke to IEEE Spectrum, "he was about an hour into his shift. Two customers had come in. Neither bought anything, although both left with free pins and stickers."

item.title: 5 Crypto Mysteries Nobody Has Solved: What's Your Theory?
item.author: Obyte
item.content:encoded: We’re far from the humble beginnings of Bitcoin, and now the crypto world is a trillion-dollar industry, full of tokens, platforms, transactions… and mysteries, too. All these years since 2009 have left us with several unsolved cases related to cryptocurrencies, and we’re not only referring to the identity of Satoshi Nakamoto or the multiple hackers who have attacked various exchanges and protocols.There’s more. Public chains can reveal where coins move, but they can’t explain every decision, identify every person behind an address, or uncover every hidden message. Let’s discover some of these puzzles, which remain unexplained to date.Bitcoin's Genesis Block MessageThis is where it all began. It turns out that not only is identity a mystery, but often, so were his motivations. We, at least, know that he was a fervent : a privacy activist, distrustful of governments and any other central parties. That’s maybe why we can find a particular embedded message in the genesis block (the first-ever block) of Bitcoin.The coinbase transaction of contains a string of hexadecimal data (alphanumeric) that, when decoded, reads “The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.” It was the headline of The Times, a British newspaper. By then, the UK government was preparing to spend more taxpayer money to rescue struggling banks during the 2008 global financial crisis.We can easily infer that it was a protest or political commentary, besides offering proof of time. A subtle hint at Bitcoin’s goal of providing an alternative to failed systems that rely on central authorities. Satoshi never talked about it, though.Were these words merely a coincidence? Just a timestamp? Probably not. In any case, many believe they offer more than one clue about the creator of Bitcoin. As we mentioned, The Times is a British newspaper, which was also sold in print. This could suggest that Satoshi was in the UK at that time, or even that he was an Englishman. However, his identity and exact motivations remain shrouded in mystery."Sleeping" Bitcoin Whale WalletsIn the early days of Bitcoin, anyone with a simple CPU could mine a lot of coins, and the price was so low that purchases reached thousands of BTC —as it happened with the first Bitcoin-bought pizza. So, even if Bitcoin wasn’t exactly a popular investment back then, some people (or groups) managed to accumulate thousands of coins.Today, they’re worth millions, and many of these early addresses have remained sleeping or “dormant” for years, without any activity on the chain. No one has been cashing out.Bitcoin isn’t exactly anonymous, but we can’t know who’s behind most of , either. So, we can’t know why the owners still have this massive fortune just sleeping, untouched for years and years. We can propose a few theories. Some may belong to early miners who forgot about their coins after Bitcoin was worth only a few cents.Others could belong to people who lost their private keys, turning vast fortunes into inaccessible digital treasure. A few owners may have chosen never to sell, treating their holdings as a long-term experiment.Others, on the other hand, make a splash every now and then and have the entire market watching their every move. in September 2025, when a long-dormant address, untouched since 2012, suddenly "resurrected" to send some funds to the exchange Kraken. It was only 5 BTC out of 955 BTC, but on other occasions, when the transaction is much larger, the entire market can suffer. That’s why everyone is watching these old whales, even if we have no idea about the identities or motivations behind them.In 2017, someone under the nickname “Pine,” who liked pineapples, decided to donate around $86 million in BTC to charity. Just like that. They opened a website dubbed “”, invited NGOs to apply for funding, and explained that, "once you have enough money, money doesn't matter." They were likely an early Bitcoin miner, but it’s not fully clear.“Sometime around the early days of bitcoin, I saw the promise of decentralized money and decided to mine/buy/trade some magical internet tokens. The expectation shattering returns of bitcoin over many years have led to an amount far more than I can spend. What do you do when you have more money than you can ever possibly spend? Donating most of it to charity is what I'm doing.”Over the following months, millions worth of Bitcoin were donated to causes ranging from clean water and medical research to environmental conservation and open-source development. The Water Project, BitGive, The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), GiveDirectly, OpenBSD, and Green Steps were just some of the projects that benefited. The campaign attracted global attention because of both its generosity and its secrecy. To this date, we still don’t know who “Pine” is. We hope they’re well!Now, if you wish to contribute as well to open-source projects, don’t forget to take a look at . By using this crypto-donation platform, you can send coins to literally any GitHub project. is the process of sending cryptocurrency to an address that nobody can access, removing those coins from circulation forever. Many networks do this on purpose to reduce supply, reward long-term holders, or support a token's economic model. Some users also burn coins voluntarily as proof of commitment, to issue new assets, or as part of technical protocols. In those cases, the reason is public, and the destruction serves a clear purpose.Not every burn comes with an explanation, though. On May 25, 2026, five Bitcoin addresses transferred 107 BTC, worth about $8.2 million at the time, to the well-known burn address 1111111111111111111114oLvT2 —making the coins permanently unspendable.The wallets in the process, while the transaction fees totaled only a few dollars. Since the transfers happened simultaneously and carried no accompanying message, they quickly became one of crypto's newest unsolved puzzles. Perhaps the most baffling bit is that they were created in 2014. So, its owner(s) held those valuable BTCs all these years... just to burn them in the end.Theories spread across the crypto community almost immediately. Some suggested the owner feared future quantum computers and chose destruction over theft. Others proposed a dead man's switch that activated automatically after years of inactivity, while another hypothesis pointed to protection against a "" or physical robbery. A simple mistake hasn't been ruled out either. The ledger records every detail of the transfers, yet it says nothing about the person behind them, leaving the motive buried along with millions of dollars in vanished Bitcoin.In case you didn’t know, anyone can engrave their own messages on most distributed ledgers —from Bitcoin to Ethereum and Obyte. The process often involves converting your message to hexadecimal code or finding specific wallets that support this function. , where you can just write something, pay the small transaction fee, and hit send. That’s how we ended up with so many “hidden” messages on different chains, forever available there for anyone curious enough to look closer at certain transactions.Some aren’t exactly mysterious. The genesis unit of Obyte says “Let there be light!” while on Bitcoin, we can find poems, ASCII art, personal notes, tributes to public figures, and even Catholic prayers from certain miners. Other inscriptions, however, consist of encrypted strings and puzzling references that appear without explanation, leaving visitors to wonder whether they were private communications, unsolved puzzles, or something else entirely.On sites like , we can explore many of these unsolved little messages. On June 26, 2026, for instance, this note appeared at the height of block 955.507: . It could, or couldn’t, be ciphertext, maybe only readable with a secret keyword. Another example happened on July 19, 2026, when someone inscribed the phrase "" on the chain. In Māori, it means “the voice is the same, the speech is the same.” What was the intention behind these inscriptions? Only the senders, and maybe the recipients, would know.Public ledgers record transactions with remarkable precision, but people remain wonderfully unpredictable. Perhaps that's why, despite all the transparency, some of crypto's greatest stories are still waiting for their final chapter.

item.title: Contact Center AI Is Moving From Demos to Audits: Inside TELUS Digital's Agent Performance Loop
item.author: sarahevans
item.content:encoded: A generative AI assistant given to more than 5,000 customer support agents raised the number of issues they resolved per hour by 15%, according to research published in. The gains landed hardest on the least experienced agents, who got faster and better at the same time.Results like that are why now puts organizational AI adoption at 88%. Most contact centers running that kind of assistance, though, cannot say whether it is doing the same thing for them. The assistant went in but the means of grading it did not.TELUS Digital, which describes itself as a CX transformation partner for Fortune 1000 brands, has organized its contact center AI work around a claim that cuts against how most of those tools were bought. Agents improve fastest when training, real-time assist and quality monitoring feed each other.Training and coaching get new agents to proficiency. Real-time agent assist gives them customer context and next-best actions during a live conversation. Quality monitoring scores every interaction against real outcomes, so supervisors see patterns across the whole operation instead of a small sample.The value comes from what moves between those stages. Suppose quality monitoring shows that one customer objection keeps costing retention saves. That pattern becomes a coaching focus and a training update, and the next time the objection comes up, the assist tool surfaces the response that has worked. Insight from one stage improves the other two.Only 32% of enterprises operating contact centers currently use AI-powered quality assurance and coaching tools, according to , a Q1 2026 study of 815 CX decision-makers across 12 countries and 19 industries. The survey also breaks down how that AI was deployed:Approach to contact center AI deploymentNative AI features inside existing CCaaS platformNative CCaaS features combined with third-party tools and custom buildsThird-party AI tools integrated with existing CCaaSFive procurement paths, five different sets of blind spots. Whichever door an enterprise came through, the grading layer was a separate purchase, and two-thirds did not make it.What makes agent assist survive production?"AI agent assist technology works in production when three things are right: the platform integrates natively with the CRM and knowledge base so agents have full customer context in a single view; the latency is low enough that recommendations and next best actions land in real time before the agent moves on; and the system captures which recommendations agents accept, ignore, or modify, aggregating those insights across all agents so the deployment keeps getting sharper at scale," Walker said.Read the list as failure modes and it gets sharper. Assist that cannot see the CRM makes the agent search twice. Assist that arrives two seconds late arrives after the agent has already started talking. Assist that never registers which suggestions get ignored will keep making the same rejected suggestion for a year.The third condition is the one most deployments skip, which is why so many plateau at the accuracy they launched with. It also depends on quality monitoring existing at all, and roughly two-thirds of the enterprises surveyed do not have it.Whatever assist recommends is a product of the data behind it. Much of what actually resolves a call lives in unannotated transcripts and in the judgment of agents who have handled the problem before. TELUS Digital's approach labels real interactions against verified business outcomes, so guidance reflects what worked in that specific operation rather than what reads well in general."Agents rarely abandon AI because the model is bad, they abandon it because it learned from the wrong data. Any vendor can sell you a model. The hard part is the data: real conversations, real workflows, real outcomes," Walker said.Continuous annotation is what keeps that current. Products change, policies change, and the questions customers ask change with them.TELUS Digital's solutions run inside its parent company, TELUS, before they reach external clients. The company calls this a that lets it refine AI-powered customer experience in real telecommunications operations. TELUS received the for its GenAI-powered customer support chatbot, built on Fuel iX, TELUS Digital's enterprise AI platform.TELUS Digital calls this its operator advantage: a client deploys a system that has already run at scale in a live contact center.The same design keeps people at the center. Under TELUS Digital's Humanity-in-the-Loop principles, AI handles lookup, customer context and routine recommendations, and agents spend more of their time on de-escalation and complex problem-solving."We are not trying to take the human out of the conversation. We are trying to make sure they have everything they need, exactly when they need it, and that a person, not a system, stays accountable for the moments that matter most, the ones that require judgment. That is what moves performance and improves your business outcomes," Walker said.CX leaders in the Strategic Advisory survey ranked customer satisfaction and service consistency as their top two AI priorities, well ahead of cost reduction. Those are the outcomes a connected loop is designed to improve, and TELUS Digital's partner guide suggests questions that test whether a partner can deliver them:Can you show training, real-time assist and quality monitoring connected and running end to end in a live operation, with results?How does your feedback loop tie agent guidance to verified business outcomes?How do you drive adoption on the contact center floor, and where do people stay accountable for high-judgment moments?The demo has stopped being the hard part. Every platform in the category will produce a convincing conversation for a prospect. The separation over the next two quarters shows up in which vendors can produce the QA record behind that conversation when a buyer asks to see it.
